Critique

Art Not Genocide Alliance, On the Making of the May 8 Strike at the 61st Venice Biennale (e-flux, 2026): The Alliance describes a 24-hour walkout by cultural workers, joined by Italian unions, in support of Palestine and workers' rights. It argues that the Biennale's governance and funding push political risk onto precarious artists and staff, enable artwashing and depend on underpaid workers. Antonia Majaca, What Did the Golden Lion Die Of? On Judgment and Disavowal at the Venice Biennale (e-flux, 2026): Majaca argues that when the 2026 jury excluded states whose leaders face International Criminal Court charges, La Biennale replaced the prize with a public vote. She links its Mussolini-era concession structure and a Qatar Museums donation for a pavilion to a spread of responsibility. See the What the field says case study.

w: Temporary exhibitions only, no permanent collection. The state government began rehabilitating the colonial building. No protest or censorship found.

f: Fundación Amparo, set up by banker Manuel Espinosa Yglesias, funds the museum. Colección FEMSA co-presents an exhibition there from 26 September 2026; the museum site names no sponsors.
w: Name to know: FEMSA. Residents of San Cristóbal de las Casas marched in April 2017 to cancel Coca-Cola FEMSA's water concession.

f: Artist-founded non-profit (Bosco Sodi, 2014); 2026 sponsors: Harp Helú, Home Depot, Teka, Grupo Habita, Tequila 1800, Punta Pájaros, Nirox Foundation.
w: Allowed money named: alcohol (Tequila 1800), retail (Home Depot), hotels/property (Grupo Habita, Punta Pájaros), banking family (Harp Helú).

f: Federal state company under Mexico's culture ministry. Modified budget MXN 132.9M for January to September 2025, of which MXN 88.0M accrued. A private patronato supports it.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. More than 250 Tijuana artists and writers boycotted the centre and its director Virgilio Muñoz for about three years, to 2011.
x: Records
The centre posts federal budget and spending reports by quarter, but no annual report, funder list or board.

f: Municipal museum of Zapopan, run through the municipal culture institute. The museum's site names no sponsors.
w: Free public contemporary art museum. The old domain mazmuseo.com now carries casino spam links; the municipal site is maz.zapopan.gob.mx.

f: Mongolian state-owned museum, created by Council of Ministers resolution in 1965 and listed under the National Centre for Cultural Heritage. No budget or sponsor list published.
w: Opened 23 July 1966 and holds over 16,000 objects. State-owned; no budget or sponsor list is published.

f: Run under Maroc Premium Foundation, which has overseen the Casablanca Biennale and the Essaouira art centre since 2014. No funder list is published.
w: Artist residency near Essaouira founded in 2008 by Mostapha Romli. The ifitry.ma site no longer resolves.

f: Structural patron NOMAD (2015 to now). Project partners 2013 to 2023: AFAC, British Council, Goethe-Institut, Pro Helvetia, US Embassy, Stimuleringsfonds, Fondation Jardin Majorelle, Kamel Lazaar Foundation.
w: Artist-run space and residency in the Marrakech medina since 2013. The partner list stops at 2023, and patron NOMAD is not identified on the site.

f: Fondation Alliances, set up in 2009 by Othman Lazraq, funds it. The Lazraq family runs the listed property developer Alliances. No other funder is named.
w: Opened 2016 in Marrakech. In April 2015 Alliances shares were suspended twice during debt talks and a conservatory seizure sought by a Holmarcom unit.

f: Sponsors in 2025: Moza Banco, Nedbank, Standard Bank and the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation. Prize partners include Óbidos council, the Portugal-Mozambique Chamber of Commerce and Camões.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. The Gulbenkian Foundation, endowed by oilman Calouste Gulbenkian, backed a 2025 drama workshop and is a listed sponsor.
x: Records
It posts activity reports for 2022 to 2025, accounts for 2019 and 2023 to 2025, a 2025 sponsor list and its three founders.
Finances
FY2025 income MZN 22.4M: about 64 percent sponsorship (Cultivarte projects, Gulbenkian, Standard Bank), 36 percent sales and rentals; no government grant line (Relatório e Contas 2025, pp. 8-10).

f: State-owned art gallery. Bank Windhoek partners on its 2025/2026 Triennial. No other sponsor is named on the site.
w: In March 2014 the gallery asked artist Paolo Solari Bozzi to withdraw photos of Himba girls; he pulled the whole show. The gallery denied censorship.

f: 2022 edition: Nepal Ministry of Culture, Prince Claus Fund, World Bank, EU, US, Australian, Swiss and Indian embassies, Toyota, Himalayan Bank. 2026: Italian Ministry of Culture grant, EUR 35,739.
w: The current supporters page lists only the organisers, so the 2022 roster is the latest full list. No excluded names on it.

f: Mondriaan Fonds and Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst fund it for 2025 to 2028. Ammodo, the city's districts, Fonds voor Cultuurparticipatie and Cultuurfonds add project money.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In 2015 the board dismissed director Lorenzo Benedetti; the Curatorial Programme tutors asked the board to resign and withdrew. An Amsterdam inquiry found the board fell short.
x: Critique

Irene De Craen, WW#14 Appels en peren (artists shown at De Appel, 2015): De Craen reads the board's 14 September 2015 dismissal of director Lorenzo Benedetti as a sign of managerial culture in the arts. She notes no visual artist sits on De Appel's board and says funding now turns on figures, citing a Mondriaan Fund application. Charles Esche, Lorenzo Benedetti deve lasciare definitivamente il De Appel. A deciderlo è La Corte del distretto di Amsterdam. Posizione che solleva una questione cruciale nel mondo dell'arte (artists shown at De Appel, 2015): Exibart reports on 4 December 2015 that the Curatorial Programme tutors, among them Esche, Filipovic, Martinez and Ruf, backed Benedetti, asked De Appel's board to resign and withdrew from the programme until it was renewed. Exibart gives no signatory count. See the What the field says case study.

f: Ministry of OCW, Amsterdams Fonds voor de Kunst, Stadsdeel Oost and VriendenLoterij Fonds, per its about page.
w: Decolonial art platform founded in 2009. The Rabo ArtLab project is in no source I opened.

f: €37.5M income (2024), City of Amsterdam 62%. VriendenLoterij is main partner; IMC, ABN AMRO, Mastercard, Polestar and Teijin are loyal partners; Ammodo and the Mondriaan Fund also give.
w: ABN AMRO is a loyal partner (2024 report). It paid €480M in 2021 to settle a Dutch money-laundering case covering 2014 to 2020.
x: Critique

Sven Lütticken, Propositional Politics (BAK, 2025): Lütticken says BAK's propositions programme grew from working inside neoliberalised Dutch funding, and faults it for never defining a proposition. He says the Stedelijk Museum relies on high-profile donors and has not answered Gaza in its programme, and he wants documenta's terms of success challenged. Not Surprised Collective, Stedelijk Museum Fails to Loan Artwork by Ahmet Ögüt to Protect Students in Amsterdam (artists shown at De Appel, 2024): Thirteen signatories say the Stedelijk refused their 28 May 2024 request to lend Ahmet Ögüt's Bakunin's Barricade to protect protesting students, offered replicas and a talk instead, and put its own interests ahead of human rights. See the What the field says case study.

f: Run by Stichting Musea Arnhem since 2014 on an annual Gemeente Arnhem subsidy (€2.6M in 2011). No sponsors named in the sources I opened.
w: Reopened on 13 May 2022 after a delayed renovation. No protest or censorship found.

f: Eindhoven municipality, Mondriaan Fund, Ammodo, Creative Europe and the Promotors foundation; VriendenLoterij, a public charity lottery, is also listed as a supporter.
w: No fossil, arms or gambling-operator funder listed. In 2011 Eindhoven councillors pushed grant cuts and a wider audience; no outcome is documented.

f: Provinsje Fryslân gives fixed subsidy; OCW and VriendenLoterij support; Windpark Fryslân is a named partner, with Fonds 21, Mondriaan Fonds, Cultuurfonds, VSBfonds, Turing and Wetterskip Fryslân.
w: Director Kris Callens left in February 2025; the museum cited transgressive behaviour. ING and ABN AMRO are not on the current partners page.

f: Gemeente Leiden, Province of South Holland and OCW fund it. Its thanks page also names BankGiro Lottery, Mondriaan Fonds, Ammodo, BNG Cultuurfonds, VSBfonds and Fonds 21.
w: The thanks page lists all donors since founding, including the tobacco-family Niemeijer Fonds, undated, so it is not counted. No protest found.

f: Province of Limburg, the culture ministry and VriendenLoterij give structural support. Mondriaan Fund, Ammodo and others add project money. Over 150,000 visitors a year.
w: Ammodo backs its 2024 to 2026 shows by Mirga-Tas and Al Solh. No protest or censorship found.

f: Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science and the Municipality of Middelburg, the two supporters named on its site. A Friends scheme takes donations.
w: No corporate sponsor or fund is named on its site. The Province of Zeeland, named in the first draft, is not listed there.

f: The Ministry of OCW, VriendenLoterij and the Helene Kröller-Müller Fonds are named in the site footer. No corporate sponsor is named.
w: The cited 2024 visitor-count page is gone; the 280,000 figure is unconfirmed. No protest or censorship found.

f: Income €2.7M (2025), €1.9M of it subsidy from Rotterdam and OCW. Ammodo, Niemeijer Fonds, Droom en Daad, Mondriaan Fonds, VSBfonds, ELJA, Elise Mathilde and Zabawas also give.
w: Flags: Tobacco, Protest or boycott. Niemeijer Fonds was founded by a Groningen tobacco manufacturer's daughter. A 2017 open letter demanded the Witte de With name go; renamed 2021.
x: Records
It posts annual reports for 2020 to 2025, the 2025 accounts, a named supervisory board and a 2025 thank-you list of funders.
Finances
FY2025 income EUR 2.7M: 70 percent subsidies, 20 percent donations and private funds, 10 percent earned and indirect income (jaarverslag 2025, staat van baten en lasten).

f: Ministry of OCW and Gemeente Rotterdam give annual support. Droom en Daad funded the Santos warehouse; the Wertheimer legacy, Fonds 21, Rabobank Rotterdam Fonds and others add project money.
w: Droom en Daad (Van der Vorm family) bought the Santos warehouse. Boijmans refused its €80M offer in 2019 after it asked for two board seats.

f: Gemeente Den Haag owns the collection and subsidises the museum. VriendenLoterij gives €500,000 a year. Mondriaan Fonds, Vereniging Rembrandt, Aronson Antiquairs and several funds also give.
w: Funds on the page include Fonds 21, Fonds1818, Turing and Debman Foundation. No regional bank, Shell, ING or BNG is named.

f: VriendenLoterij has backed the museum since 2008 and paid €579,767 in 2025. Stichting Abramsen-Koedam co-presents its sculpture prize. Friends and Rabo ClubSupport votes add income.
w: The researcher's BNG, Aegon and other names come from 2018 and 2019 reports, so they are not current. BNG is state-owned; no protest found.

f: Private museum run by a foundation built on the estate of Jan de Pont. It takes no municipal subsidy and sought no government or fund support.
w: Nearly 75,000 visitors in 2023. De Pont was a lawyer and businessman linked to Tilburg's wool industry. No sponsor named.

f: Basecamp funders: ELJA Foundation, Fonds 21, het Cultuurfonds, K.F. Hein Fonds, Municipality of Utrecht, DOEN/VriendenLoterij Fonds, VSBfonds. Utrecht ended its multi-year subsidy in 2024.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Utrecht ended its multi-year subsidy from 2025 despite a positive advisory report, BAK says; the Council for Culture advised ending state funding. Four post-academic institutions wrote in support.
x: Critique

Sven Lütticken, Propositional Politics (BAK, 2025): Lütticken says BAK's propositions programme grew from working inside neoliberalised Dutch funding, and faults it for never defining a proposition. He says the Stedelijk Museum relies on high-profile donors and has not answered Gaza in its programme, and he wants documenta's terms of success challenged. See the What the field says case study.

f: Structural support from Mondriaan Fund, City of Utrecht and Stichting DOEN via Arts Collaboratory.
w: The site names no corporate sponsor and gives no years for the support. No protest or censorship found.

f: Gemeente Utrecht, VriendenLoterij and the Ministry of OCW are named on the museum's sponsor page. No corporate sponsor is named.
w: The page gives no amounts or dates for the three. No protest or censorship found.

f: Creative New Zealand (NZ$637k a year for 2027 to 2029) and Auckland Council lead; strategic partners are Chartwell Trust, Foundation North, Goethe-Institut and Wesfarmers.
w: Wesfarmers is mostly Bunnings and Kmart; its chemicals, energy and fertilisers division, which holds gas retailer Kleenheat, is about 5 percent of group revenue.

f: 497,998 visitors (2024-25). Run by Tātaki Auckland Unlimited for Auckland Council. Partners include BMW, Van Cleef & Arpels, HSBC, Anthony Harper, Baker Tilly; trusts include Chartwell and Mackelvie.
w: HSBC backed A Century of Modern Art in 2025. HSBC agreed a $1.92 billion US penalty in December 2012 over money-laundering failures.

f: Core funding from the Waitākere Ranges Local Board (Auckland Council). It also takes gifts from a Benefactors Collective and sponsors, none named.
w: Its site names no sponsor or trust. Income was NZ$1.17M in the year to June 2024.

f: Christchurch City Council; the Christchurch Art Gallery Foundation raises acquisition funds. Partners are JBWere (foundation partner) and Anthony Harper (major partner), plus hotel, design and drinks suppliers.
w: No gaming-machine trust, SkyCity or fossil company is listed on the support page.

f: Dunedin City Council gallery. Gallery Partners are Creative New Zealand, Quartz Reef and Craigs Investment Partners; the DPAG Society buys works.
w: Founding partners in 1996 included Mobil Oil New Zealand and the Lotteries Board; neither is a current funder.

f: Hutt City Council provides most funding. The Dowse Foundation, set up in 2003, raised $2M. Corporate partners in 2025: Dulux, Tuatara Brewery, Almighty.
w: The Foundation's founding partners, from its 2003 campaign, include NZ Community Trust and Pub Charity, gaming-machine trusts; no current gaming-trust funding found.

f: NZ$85M revenue (2024-25), Crown 52%. Its current partners page lists Panasonic, Bloomberg, Samsung, MyLotto and gaming-machine trusts PubCharity and Lion Foundation.
w: Flags: Gambling. Both raise money from gaming machines. Named Te Taiao | Nature grant partners at its 2019 opening and again in the 2024-25 annual report.

It posts annual reports from 2000-01 to 2024-25 with Auditor-General accounts, names its eight board members and lists partners without a date.
Finances
FY2024-25 revenue NZD 85.0M: about 52 percent Crown funding, 6 percent donations and sponsorship, 32 percent commercial, exhibition and rental revenue (annual report 2024/25, p. 36 and note 3).

f: Whanganui District Council ($26.1M) led the NZ$79.4M rebuild with the Ministry for Culture and Heritage, Lottery Grants Board, Provincial Growth Fund, Stout Trust and other unnamed trusts.
w: Nearly NZ$11M came from community and private trusts and individuals, mostly unnamed. No Lion Foundation, Pub Charity, NZCT or SkyCity is named.

f: Founded 2007 by Bisi Silva with her own money. A March 2022 Sotheby's benefit auction raised US$1M toward a permanent home in Yaba. It publishes no funder list.
w: Its site names no donors or partners. The claim of foundation-only funding, never Nigerian state or corporate money, has no source.

f: Federal Government through the National Commission for Museums and Monuments; IHS Nigeria, a telecom-tower company, funded a 2026 renovation. A Ford Foundation refit stalled.
w: Reopened April 2026 after renovation. No NNPC, Shell, TotalEnergies or Dangote money found.

f: Ministry of Culture, City of Bergen, Vestland county, Arts Council Norway, Fritt Ord, Sparebanken Norge, Nordic Council of Ministers, Bergesen Foundation, Westfal-Larsen fund and EGD Holding.
w: No Equinor, Aker, Fredriksen, Norsk Tipping or other flag-category funder is named on its supporter list.

f: 2025 income: 59% public grants (including state budget and Bærum municipality), 9% sponsors, 16% project gifts, 17% own revenue. Main partners: Sparebankstiftelsen DNB and DNV (NOK 2M a year).
w: DNV, formerly DNV GL, serves the oil and gas industry. DNV GL halted Nord Stream 2 certification work in November 2020 after US sanctions threats.

f: Christen Sveaas, his investment company Kistefos AS and Christen Sveaas' art foundation; Riksantikvaren, local and county councils and savings-bank foundations.
w: Kistefos AS invests in offshore services, shipping, banks and property. Oilfield and supply services are no flag.

f: Norwegian Ministry of Culture and Equality, the Thomas Fearnley, Heddy and Nils Astrup and Hans Rasmus Astrup foundations, and Sparebankstiftelsen DNB; sponsors EGD Holding and The Thief.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. Lundin Norway, an oil company, was main sponsor 2012 to 2019. Kunstkritikk's editor called it image laundering; its Swedish editor cancelled a lecture there.

The museum posts no annual report, but its accounts are in Norway's register, its board is named and funders and sponsors are listed undated.
Finances
FY2025 operating income NOK 70.8M, of which 32 percent is sales revenue; the register summary does not split the other 68 percent between state grant, foundation gifts and sponsors.

f: Ministry of Culture and Oslo municipality operating grants. Sparebankstiftelsen DNB gave NOK 40M in 2024 to start rehabilitation. Fritt Ord and Bergesenstiftelsen also give.
w: The foundation needs NOK 186M to rehabilitate the building before its 100th anniversary in 2030.

f: Ministry of Culture and Equality, Stavanger municipality, Kulturdirektoratet (Arts Council Norway) and Rogaland county, plus Fritt Ord, Bergesenstiftelsen and Sparebankstiftelsen SR-bank.
w: Supporters come from the About page. No annual accounts with figures were found.

f: Punjab and federal government bodies; lead sponsor Habib Bank; star sponsors Barjeel Art Foundation, Bareeze and ICCI; partners include Nishat, PIA, Dulux and Careem.
w: The sponsor page is undated and shows logos only. No oil, gas, arms, tobacco or gambling sponsor is listed; no censorship or boycott found.

f: Building (about US$24M, 2016) paid by 30-plus Palestinian families, Qattan Foundation, Bank of Palestine and the Arab Fund; Aliph funded a 2022 studio. No current donor list.
w: Independent of Taawon since 2021. The claim that it takes no Palestinian Authority money has no source.

f: Sponsored by Al Risan Art Museum. It aimed to raise $90,000 for its artists through institutional partnerships and donations (2024). The Istanbul pavilion ran on private and artist support.
w: Artist-led project launched in 2024 with over 60 Palestinian artists. In January 2025 it protested Bloomberg Philanthropies' funding of the ICA's New Contemporaries.

f: Income GBP 2.6M (2025): Al-Qattan Charitable Trust, Qattan family gifts, Save the Children, Drosos, Taawon, Enabel, Arts Council England, Art Fund.
w: Barclays (under campaign) is one of its bankers, not a funder. Trust funding paused in 2025 pending a Jersey licence, not as punishment.

f: Riwaq NGO: EU, Sweden, Germany/KfW, UNDP, UNESCO, ALIPH, British Council CPF, Ford, Open Society, Prince Claus, Doen, Arab Fund, OPEC Fund.
w: OPEC Fund for International Development (oil-state money) is on Riwaq's donor list. Last full biennale 2014; 2019 Chicago edition.

n: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Panamá
f: Private non-profit funded by companies and art lovers. Naturgy, a gas and electricity group, signed a sponsorship in April 2023 covering upkeep and operations.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Naturgy is a gas utility group; its Panama arm distributes electricity. Donor logos on the museum's site carry no names.

Publishes annual reports for 2018 to 2025 and a named board; donor logos carry no names or date, and no financial statements are posted.

f: Private foundation museum (Escobar, Salerno); 2026 sponsors page names Banco Itaú, Citibank, French embassy, a law firm and named friends.
w: Bank money named: Itaú (sponsor) and Citibank (supporter). No sponsor controversy found.

f: Private museum in Barranco; sponsors include Fundación Telefónica, Fundación BBVA, Credicorp, UTEC, EU delegation, Getty Foundation, Bloomberg.
w: Bloomberg is listed as a sponsor. It is under active campaign elsewhere; the atlas lists Bloomberg-roster institutions as B. No protest found at MAC Lima.

f: KPMG-audited 2025 revenue S/17.1M: tuition 38%, donations and memberships 37%, services 25%. Donors named: Fundación Telefónica, JOMA, THOMA, Smurfit Kappa. Camisea gas consortium funded free Thursdays.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Camisea, operated by Pluspetrol, sponsored free Thursday entry from August 2022 to March 2025. Alberto Rebaza chairs the board.

Posts audited accounts for 2003 to 2025, committee annual reports for 2007 to 2021 and a named board; its partners page shows an unnamed banner.
Finances
FY2025 income PEN 17.1M: about 38 percent tuition, 37 percent donations and memberships, 25 percent rentals and services; a government capital grant of PEN 987k was released (audited statements).

n: Museum of Contemporary Art and Design (MCAD)
f: Part of De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde. It relies on Art Circle patrons and benefit auctions (Funding the Future, 2018 and 15 November 2025). Donors are not named.
w: Free, non-collecting museum. Leon Gallery is the auction partner and artists donate the works.

f: University museum of Ateneo de Manila University, founded 1960 on Fernando Zobel's gift of his collection; later donors, including artists, added works.
w: Zobel gave his artwork collection. No operating funder, sponsor, protest or censorship flag is documented.

f: Formerly central-bank subsidised; now a non-profit foundation (1979, Imelda Marcos, Bienvenido Tantoco Sr.). Founding benefactors include Campos family firms NutriAsia and Del Monte Philippines; Metrobank and NCCA back programmes.

n: KALEKTAR research platform on Belarusian contemporary art
f: German Federal Foreign Office (Civil Society Cooperation programme) and Rönne-Stiftung, per the platform's own about page
w: Online archive, index and journal founded 2015; co-founder and editor-in-chief Sergey Shabohin lives and works in Białystok, which is used as the map point since the platform publishes no address.

f: Municipal museum of the City of Kraków. Its partners page names Strabag as museum sponsor, with Remondis, RE-Bau, Tribe Hotels and the Ministry of Culture.
w: Sponsor Strabag's minority shareholder Rasperia was controlled by Oleg Deripaska, sanctioned by the US, EU and UK. Strabag keeps the stake frozen (2025).

f: European Union (ArtPower Belarus, €2M over 28 months, delivered with the Danish Cultural Institute); Danish Cultural Institute; listed partners ABBA, RESET!, Forum of National Platforms, NDF
w: Founded 1 Oct 2020 as the Belarusian Culture Solidarity Fund, renamed Feb 2021; registered in Tallinn as MTÜ Valgevene Kultuuri Assotsiatsioon and represented in Warsaw and Vilnius; CEO Siarhiej Budkin. f: Ticket sales; an actor says funding is zero (2025). Polish Ministry of Culture award (March 2025); Latushka's foundation backs two projects; Council of Culture passes on EU money.

f: National cultural institution financed by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage; some projects co-financed from the state budget and the EU.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. A 2019 art-world petition opposed director Piotr Bernatowicz's appointment; crowds protested his 'Political Art' show in August 2021. The minister dismissed him in June 2024.

Publishes no annual reports or accounts that we found; the partners page shows logos with no dates and the board is not listed.

f: 2025 budget PLN 9.6M: 76% base grant including the city's, 13% earmarked grants, 8% national grant programmes (Ministry of Culture), 2% own revenue, 0% outside sponsors.
w: Municipal gallery network of the City of Wrocław. The Adam Mickiewicz Institute funded its Milan Triennale show in 2025.

f: Cultural institution of the Łódź Voivodeship self-government, co-financed by the Minister of Culture and National Heritage. It seeks paying partners through its 'partner ms' programme.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. Culture ministry dismissed director Jarosław Suchan in April 2022 with no explanation; Guggenheim, MoMA and Tate directors and Polish artists protested in letters.

Posts activity reports for 2016 to 2025, profit and loss accounts for 2016 to 2023 and its 15-member museum council; no named funder list.

Calendar 2023 income PLN 26.0M: about 94 percent public subsidies (budget subsidy 16.9M plus other grants 7.6M), 4 percent sales of goods; no donations line (profit and loss account).

f: Caixa Geral de Depósitos (state bank) gave EUR 6.45M in 2025, EUR 3.2M for operations. Own revenue of EUR 2.27M came from Fidelidade, EU funds, patrons, tickets and rentals.

f: Founders Ferré-Rangel and Fonalledas families and Fundación Ángel Ramos; 700+ individuals; gala sponsors led by Banco Popular, including Genera PR (New Fortress Energy) in 2023 and Puma Energy in 2019.

FY2024-25 income USD 16.2M: about 58 percent government grants, 37 percent other donations and gifts, under 1 percent earned; investment income is 529k (Form 990, Part VIII).

n: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico
f: Non-profit (EIN 66-0420190); 2026 funders: NEA, IMLS, Luce, Wallace, Teiger, Banco Popular, Walmart, PR Tourism Co., The Macallan.
w: Moved to museomac.org. Names alcohol (The Macallan), retail (Walmart) and bank (Banco Popular) money. No controversy found.

f: 2023: no permanent private or state funding and no annual budget, per its programme director. In 2017 patron Rinat Mardanov and landlord Yakov Margulis paid for launch and reconstruction.

n: Moscow International Biennale of Contemporary Art
f: Private biennale foundation (Yulia Muzykantskaya); sponsor roster not published; 2022 edition hosted by the state Tretyakov Gallery.

f: Moscow city government, through the Department of Culture, since the 1999 opening. Founder Zurab Tsereteli died in April 2025. Patron and donor programme; no sponsor names published.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Cancelled a student show in July 2022 over 'political subtext'; iStories says Culture Department orders reached curators, and artists' works were painted over.

Posts a 2025 results report and balance sheets for 2015 to 2025, but names no sponsors or board; only management is listed.
Finances
Calendar 2025 income RUB 714.5M: about 94 percent Moscow city subsidies, 6 percent paid services, under 1 percent gratuitous receipts (plan execution reports, form 0503737).

f: Founded by Boris Mints (O1 Group), who cannot fund it as before. Trustee Vladimir Voronin (FSK Group) since Feb 2024. About 40% of budget is admissions (2023); rest partners, donors.
w: National Bank Trust, 99% owned by Russia's central bank, sues founder Boris Mints and sons for $850m in London; they deny fraud.

n: Arsenal, Volga-Vyatka branch of the Pushkin Museum
f: Federal via the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts (branch since 2020); three-year cooperation agreement with Nizhny Novgorod region signed 15 Nov 2024.
w: Founder-director Anna Gor became a Pushkin deputy director; Alexander Komarov now heads the branch. No local sponsor list.

f: Artist-run autonomous non-profit founded 2015 by Artem Filatov; grants, ticket/catalogue sales and donated artworks; a Garage Museum grant funds its archive.
w: Nine resident artists; collaborates with Garage on archiving the Nizhny Novgorod scene.

f: Regional state (GKBUK; founder Ministry of Culture of Perm Krai); founded 2009 under governor Chirkunov with Marat Gelman and sponsor Sergei Gordeev; new building on Krisanova St since 2024.
w: FSB searched the museum and director Nailya Allakhverdieva's home on 21 Nov 2024 in the 'terrorism justification' case against founder Gelman (declared foreign agent 2021, listed as terrorist/extremist 2024); museum closed one day. Prosecutor filed a conflict-of-interest suit against the director in Oct 2024; an earlier search in Mar 2024. Allakhverdieva left; Elena Novikova appointed.

f: Perm Krai government; its Ministry of Culture is founder. Sber is general partner of the opening season and the Potanin Foundation backs a 2026-2028 programme.
w: Flags: Sanctions. Sber is on US, EU and UK sanctions lists. Vladimir Potanin, whose foundation backs the programme, is sanctioned by the US and UK.
x: Records
Posts a 2025 results report and 2025 financial results report, with plans back to 2022; no sponsor list and no board.
Finances
Calendar 2025 income RUB 261.4M: about 98 percent Perm Krai subsidies (156M of it for other purposes), 1 percent paid services, 1 percent gratuitous receipts (2025 execution report).

f: Private: founded 2010 by Marina Varvarina (widow of Orimi tea-and-coffee group owner Dmitry Varvarin); the museum states it has never taken state support, grants or sponsors.
w: 12,000 sq m, c. 40 exhibitions a year; c. US$30–35m invested in the building. No sanctions match for Varvarina on OpenSanctions.

f: St Petersburg city budget institution under the Committee for Culture. Its site lists partners and sponsors including PhosAgro, VTB Bank, PSB, Rosseti Lenenergo and Bank Saint Petersburg.
w: Flags: Sanctions, Arms and defence, State censorship or punishment. Treasury sanctioned VTB and PSB in 2022; PSB finances Russia's defense industry. Artists told Novaya Gazeta Manege barred or retitled works in 2024.
x: Records
Names partners and sponsors in text with no date and lists a four-member supervisory board; posts only a 2025 task report and a financial plan.

f: Self-managed artists' commune since 1989 under the Free Culture Fellowship. No funder list is published; it gave its collection of about 5,000 items to the state in 2023.
w: Founders Rybakov and Orlov told Novaya Gazeta that Manege barred one work and demanded a retitle for another in the 2024 show.

f: Founded 2013 by Alexander Mechetin, co-owner of the Novabev Group (spirits); Novabev lists Zarya in its corporate responsibility programme. Partners include the State Tretyakov Gallery.
w: Novabev is a spirits group; alcohol is not a flag category. OpenSanctions search shows no sanctions entry for Mechetin or Novabev.

f: State budgetary institution of Voronezh Oblast, run on annual state assignments. The federal 'Culture' national project paid for storage cabinets in 2023.
w: Governor Aleksandr Gusev heads the funding region; he is on US (2023), EU (2023) and UK (2024) sanctions lists.

n: Ural Industrial Biennial of Contemporary Art
f: State: Ural branch of the National Centre for Contemporary Arts, part of the Pushkin Museum since 2020; 6th edition (2021) budget c. 100m RUB; residencies sought Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives grants.
w: 7th edition cancelled in Apr 2023 (announced by the city administration without explanation); team shifted to a research platform and art-industrial routes (2025 routes to Nov 2025). Founder-commissioner Alisa Prudnikova left to run GES-2 (V-A-C).

f: City of Yekaterinburg: the Department of Culture of the city administration is founder of this municipal autonomous museum. Financial reports for 2014-2024 are published; no sponsor list.
w: Five sites including the Hermitage-Ural centre; a supervisory board oversees the museum. Financial reports are scanned images.

f: Financed by the Senegalese state through the culture ministry; its sponsors page names the Prime Minister's office, City of Dakar, UNESCO, ECOWAS, Ecobank, SUNU Group and Sococim (cement).
w: The 16th edition runs 19 November to 19 December 2026. The 2024 edition was postponed, drawing criticism from artists and curators; no sponsor flag.

f: Senegalese state museum. China financed the building with a CFA 20 billion (over EUR 30M) grant. 2025 own revenue was CFA 353.9M.
w: China's grant paid for the building, not operations. No sponsor, protest or censorship found.

f: Founded 2008 by Koyo Kouoh. Partners listed for 2024: Arts Collaboratory, OSIWA, Mellon Foundation, Foundation for Arts Initiatives, Little Sun, Porticus and Sharjah Art Foundation.
w: Flags: Gulf state body. Sharjah Art Foundation, a Sharjah government body, is already flagged Gulf state body on this map.
x: Records
Site unreachable; its 2024 programme announcement names Arts Collaboratory, Osiwa, Mellon, Foundation for Arts Initiatives, Little Sun, Porticus and Sharjah Art Foundation.

n: NTU Centre for Contemporary Art Singapore
f: Co-funded by Nanyang Technological University and Singapore's Economic Development Board (2020 reports). SEA AiR residency funded by the European Union.
w: Closed its Gillman Barracks exhibition and residency space in March 2021 after financial restructuring; continues as an NTU research centre.

f: Singapore government base grant of S$1.2m a year, about 30% of costs, plus a rent-free state building (2016, per director). Rest from artwork sales and patrons.
w: Latest funding statement found is the director's 2016 interview. STPI publishes no donor list or accounts; patron tiers start at S$2,500.

f: FY23/24: state (Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth) plus Mapletree, Singapore Tourism Board, CHARLES & KEITH Foundation, New Carlsberg Foundation (alcohol).
w: Board member Pierre Lorinet is a director of oil trader Trafigura (joined 1 Jul 2024). Roster is from FY23/24; the FY24/25 report was not found.

n: MGLC International Centre of Graphic Arts
f: Public institute founded by the City of Ljubljana, funded from its budget. 36th Biennale (2025) backed by the Ministry of Culture, Pro Helvetia, Mondriaan Fund and Danish Arts Foundation.
w: Organises the Ljubljana Biennale of Graphic Arts. Its 2025 edition lists TBA21 and Schering Stiftung as partners, and Delo and Kaval Group among local backers.

f: Slovenian Ministry of Culture: up to EUR 2.07m from the state budget for its 2022 programme, plus up to EUR 100,000 for the Venice Biennale pavilion.
w: Founded by government decree in 1947 as the national museum of modern art. Its site has no sponsor page.

f: National public entity, an agency of the Department of Arts and Culture (now Sport, Arts and Culture). No corporate sponsor is named on its site.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. In December 2025 management covered 11 works in Steven Cohen's retrospective the night before opening. SWEAT and Sisonke protested Mthethwa's work in December 2016.
x: Records
Posts annual reports from 2003/04 to 2025/26 with audited statements and donor sections, and names its nine-member council; the site itself lists no donors.
Finances
FY2025-26 revenue ZAR 239.6M for Iziko Museums of South Africa, the gallery's parent: about 54 percent government grants, 33 percent state property in kind, 3 percent sponsorship, 6 percent earned.

f: Property investor Louis Norval financed it entirely at the 2018 opening and set up a capital fund. Sponsors include Schroders (art prize), Stonehage Fleming (2021 auction) and Sanlam.
w: A capital fund and earned income are meant to make it self-sustaining. No fossil, arms or gambling sponsor found.

f: Jochen Zeitz donated the collection he had loaned; sponsors include Gucci and BMW, the Mellon Foundation funds fellowships, and the board now pays.
w: Director Mark Coetzee resigned in 2018 amid misconduct allegations and sued; this concerns staff, not a funder or board figure.

f: Owned and run by the City of Johannesburg; no corporate sponsor is named. Joburg Heritage Foundation and Friends of JAG back a funded rescue plan.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Joburg Heritage Foundation and Friends of JAG sent the City a legal demand in August 2024 and weighed an interdict in January 2025.
x: Records
Publishes no annual reports, accounts, funders or board of its own; the City of Johannesburg runs the gallery and the Heritage Foundation posts rescue updates.

f: Wits campus museum, opened 2006; its Rock Art Research Institute is funded by the National Research Foundation, Wits' research fund and Anglo American's Chairman's Fund. No centre funder list.
w: No page names a donor or sponsor of the centre itself. The draft's Arcadia and arts-department funding has no source.

f: University of the Witwatersrand museum. Standard Bank has been collection partner since 1978 and 1979; early donors include Norman Herber, Jack Ginsberg, John Schlesinger and Gertrude Posel.
w: No fossil, arms or gambling sponsor named. The May 2024 Wits encampment concerned university policy, not this museum.

f: 2026 edition run by the Busan Biennale Organizing Committee for Busan Metropolitan City, with BNK Busan Bank, Shinsegae, Naver and Danish, Dutch and UK cultural funds.
w: Bank (BNK Busan Bank), retail (Shinsegae) and media (Naver) money named; no sponsor protest found in English or Korean searches.

f: Municipal museum run by Busan Metropolitan City, reopened in 2026 after a 46.9bn-won rebuild; patrons' society members include BNK Busan Bank and Hwaseung Group.
w: Curatorial dispute, Sept 2026: Korea Economic Daily called its reopening exhibition on defector and socialist-affiliated artists one-sided.

f: Busan Metropolitan City: its ordinance names the mayor as operator. Free entry except special shows, capped at 15,000 won. Opened June 2018.
w: Museum on Eulsukdo; second director Kang Seung-wan since June 2022. Its site menu has no sponsor page.

f: 2024: hosted by Changwon City and Changwon Culture Foundation; backed by Culture Ministry, Gyeongnam Province, KICOX, BNK Kyongnam Bank, Gyeongnam Mecenat Association. 2026 host unchanged.
w: 2024 edition drew 107,710 visitors. The 2026 edition runs 30 Sep to 15 Nov; its supporter list was not found.

f: Executive agency of South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism since 2015. Its planning division builds and spends the state budget; the ACC Foundation shares operations.
w: Opened November 2015 in Gwangju. Its site menu has no sponsor or donor page.

f: Non-profit association (2019); 2026 shows supported by Arts Council Korea, supervised by Seoul Metropolitan Government, plus individual LOOP's Friends donors.
w: Dec 2025 Euljiro move drew a public gentrification inquiry from Cheonggyecheon-Euljiro Preservation Alliance and others.

f: Corporate museum run directly by Amorepacific Corp (site footer, 2026); cosmetics money. Current LeWitt show co-organised with MOT Tokyo.
w: Single funder: Amorepacific cosmetics. No sponsor protest found.

f: Private museum founded by collector Kim Chang-il (CI Kim), funded by his Arario Corporation (bus terminal, retail, galleries).
w: Founder-funder Kim Chang-il got a 2-year sentence for breach of duty (Daejeon court, Feb 2021); the group said it would appeal.

f: State-run: operated by Arts Council Korea (national arts body, est. 1973) alongside its theatres and archive; no corporate sponsors listed.
w: Parent Arts Council Korea gave grant juries a political blacklist of artists in 2015; exposed in a National Assembly inspection.

f: Private museum founded 1998. Its site links the Daewoo Foundation, funded mainly by Daewoo chairman Kim Woo Choong since 1978, and invites corporate sponsors but names no funders.
w: No source ties the Daewoo Foundation to the centre's budget, and no sponsor list is published.

f: Run by the Ilmin Cultural Foundation, a non-profit founded in 1994 in memory of Dong-A Ilbo president Kim Sang-man; the newspaper entrusted works to the collection.
w: No budget, donor or sponsor list found. The draft's newspaper-family funds claim has no source.

f: State museum. Hyundai Motor sponsored its series from 2014 to February 2024; LG Electronics sponsors the OLED Series from 2025. The Lee Kun-hee estate gave nearly 1,500 works in 2021.
w: Flags: Forced or exploited labour. Hyundai Motor sponsored its series to February 2024. Reuters found children as young as 12 at Hyundai subsidiary SMART Alabama in 2022.
x: Records
The state museum posts no annual report, accounts, sponsor list or board on its site; its sponsorship page points to a separate foundation site.

f: Seoul Metropolitan Government museum; Hana Financial Group co-funds SeMA-Hana Art Award; patrons' association SeMA人[in] since 2014.
w: June 2025 censorship row (critic's martial-law essay cut from catalogue). Patrons' board includes SK Group and MBK Partners.

f: Private museum run by the Whanki Foundation, set up by the artist's widow Kim Hyang-an. No funder list or accounts found; the museum site fails its certificate check.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In May 2026 residents and the Seoul Environment Alliance protested after herbicide was injected into a 200-year-old ginkgo beside the museum. It apologised.
x: Records
Could not check: the museum site fails its security certificate and no register entry for the Whanki Foundation could be opened.

f: Gyeonggi Province, through the Gyeonggi Cultural Foundation. Hyundai Motor sponsors its Trans-Local exhibition series (KRW 600M over three years, announced 2025). Free admission.
w: Flags: Forced or exploited labour. Hyundai subsidiary SMART Alabama hired children as young as 12 (Reuters, 2022). Same Hyundai ruling as MMCA applies.
x: Records
Its parent foundation posts yearbooks for 2012 to 2025, settlement papers and a named board; the centre shows sponsor logos only, undated.

f: 2025 grants EUR 2.76m: Spanish Ministry of Culture 1.17m, Generalitat de Catalunya 0.88m, Barcelona City Council 0.52m, Diputacio de Barcelona 0.15m. Budgeted income EUR 3.50m.
w: Grants are 79% of 2025 budgeted income. Trustees include the artist's family and Generalitat and city appointees.

f: Private foundation; Generalitat, Barcelona council and Culture Ministry sit on its board. Strategic allies: Fundación BBVA, Fundació la Caixa, Puig. Also Fundació Banc Sabadell, Abertis, Sorigué, Damm.
w: la Caixa's holding Criteria is the largest shareholder of gas utility Naturgy, which paid 23% of Criteria's 2025 dividends.

f: Private museum run by the Chillida family. Hauser & Wirth, which represents the estate, gave financial support for the 2019 reopening. Gipuzkoa council lent storage during works; no sponsors named.
w: Corporate sponsor page lists tiers from EUR 2,000 a year but no names. Partial closure from 2011 over a recurring deficit; full reopening April 2019.

f: State museum. Corporate patrons: Inditex, Fundación la Caixa, Fundación Mapfre, Fundación Mutua Madrileña. Partners include Estrella Damm, HP, Iberia, Madrid city and region.
w: la Caixa's holding Criteria is the largest shareholder of gas utility Naturgy, 23% of its 2025 dividends. No Repsol, Endesa or Iberdrola listed.

f: 3.5M visitors (2025). Benefactors Fundación BBVA (2025) and Fundación AXA (2024); Fundación Iberdrola España funds fellowships to 2027; Fundación Endesa, Rassini and la Caixa (to 2025) fund projects.
w: Utilities Iberdrola (66% renewable capacity) and Endesa fund programmes; both sell gas. la Caixa's holding Criteria owns 28.5% of gas utility Naturgy.

n: CA2M Centro de Arte Dos de Mayo
f: Comunidad de Madrid, as a museum of its Culture, Tourism and Sport department: 2024 budget EUR 1.45m for programming plus EUR 500,000 for art purchases.
w: Staff are employees of the regional culture department. Holds the Comunidad de Madrid collection and the Fundacion ARCO collection. No sponsor list published.

f: Govern balear, Consell de Mallorca, Palma council and Fundació d'Art Serra form the foundation. Sponsors: Fundació Baleària, Caixa Colonya, El Corte Inglés, Summum Hotel Group, Hotel Saratoga.
w: Sponsor names come from the collaborators page. No energy, tobacco, arms or gambling name appears. No protest or censorship found.

f: Public company owned by Donostia city council, Gipuzkoa council and the Basque Government, five board seats each. 2025 income EUR 1.87m; Basque culture department nominal grants.
w: Former state tobacco factory (1913-2003), bought by the three bodies. Its 2025 annual report names no tobacco company.

f: 2024: Diputacion Foral de Alava EUR 2.53m, Basque Government EUR 1.72m, Spanish Ministry of Culture EUR 150,000, Vitoria-Gasteiz city EUR 130,000.
w: Run by a foundation; the Alava council owns the building. The Basque Government gave EUR 200,000 in 2024 for Shared Collection purchases.

f: Run by the independent Fold Media Collective. Named: founding partners Goethe-Institut, British Council and Alliance Française, plus individual Friends. The page's 33 partner and patron logos carry no names.
w: Cinnamon Hotels was title sponsor in the 2010s. The Gujral Foundation is a long-term partner. The ASAP grant in the old text is not found.

n: Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art Sri Lanka
f: Non-profit set up in 2019, with no fixed venue. Founding Patrons are individuals; the John Keells Foundation was named primary sponsor in March 2020.
w: John Keells Holdings, the foundation's parent, developed the City of Dreams Sri Lanka resort (opened August 2025); Melco manages the casino with JKH.

f: Run by Lund municipality's culture and leisure committee. The municipal council approved an SEK 86M rebuild in Aug 2026, with the hall closed for 18 months.
w: No sponsors or private funders are listed. The site states it is part of Lund municipality. No funder controversy found.

f: Part of Malmö stad's culture department and funded by the city. The Swedish Inheritance Fund (Allmänna Arvsfonden) gave SEK 6M for the Studio Syd artist centre, 2025-27.
w: Free entry. No sponsors are listed on its site. No funder controversy found.

f: Run non-profit under the Bonnier Group. The Jeanette Bonnier Foundation, set up after her death in 2016, supports its financing and development.
w: Grew out of the Maria Bonnier Dahlin Foundation, founded 1985 by Jeanette Bonnier. Its site lists no outside sponsors.

f: Robert Weil Family Foundation, funded by the Weil family office Proventus. No outside sponsors or public funders are named on the museum or foundation sites.
w: Founded 1987 by David Neuman and Robert Weil. Runs a Jaffa branch since 2018. No protest or censorship found.

f: SEK 271M income (2025), state 70%. Sponsors: Bank of America, Bloomberg, PwC, Jung, Patriksson and an unnamed wine and spirits supplier; partners Hotel Skeppsholmen and Panasonic Connect.
w: Sponsor Bloomberg: more than 260 UK artists asked five London theatres to drop Bloomberg Philanthropies in May 2026. Moderna Museet was not named.

f: 2022 income SEK 37.3m: Umeå University 22.6m, Umeå municipality 5.0m, Fort Knox 3.0m, Culture Ministry 0.8m, Region Västerbotten 0.5m.
w: University museum of Umeå University. Umeå municipality gave SEK 5.0m in both 2019 and 2022; Fort Knox is credited on named exhibitions.

f: Canton Basel-Stadt CHF 950k a year for 2024-27 (32% of budget); third-party grants about CHF 660k (30%); restaurant and property rent 22%; members 8%.
w: In November 2023 an SVP member of the cantonal parliament demanded subsidy be cut over director Almusibli's ceasefire letters; the canton did not act.

f: Canton Basel-Stadt and the Emanuel Hoffmann, Christoph Merian and Laurenz foundations. UBS is partner; Novartis, KPMG, Trafina and the Federal Office of Culture are sponsors.
w: UBS paid a $100M Federal Reserve fine in 2004 over dollar dealings with sanctioned states. Novartis paid $678M in 2020 over kickbacks to doctors.

f: Roche has paid all operating costs since the museum opened in 1996 as a gift for its centenary; Roche built it and funds collection additions.
w: Roche pleaded guilty in 1999 to a worldwide vitamin price-fixing conspiracy and paid $500M in US criminal fines.

f: Made possible by the Laurenz Foundation, founded in 1999 by Maja Oeri and Hans U. Bodenmann. The foundation does not give grants; no other funders are named.
w: Herzog & de Meuron built it in 2002-03. The Emanuel Hoffmann Foundation collection is its core.

f: City of Bern pays CHF 1.05M a year (83% of 2025 income). Foundations back shows: Scherbarth, Guggenheim, Gubler-Hablützel. Burgergemeinde Bern and the canton's lottery fund supported building work.
w: 2023: two city-council factions asked about the incoming director's signed Palestine letter. The city grant stayed CHF 1.05M.

f: Canton Bern and the Burgergemeinde's museum foundation fund it. UBS is main sponsor; Mobiliar and UNIQA sponsor exhibitions; eight funding foundations include Hansjörg Wyss's Stiftung GegenwART.
w: UBS paid a $100M US Federal Reserve fine in 2004 for dollar trading with Iran and other sanctioned countries.

f: Canton of Fribourg, City and Agglomeration of Fribourg, Loterie Romande, Banque Cantonale de Fribourg, the Sandoz family foundation and the Friends association.
w: Loterie Romande is a public lottery, no flag. Partners include the University of Fribourg and Fribourg Tourisme. No protest or censorship found.

f: Canton Basel-Landschaft, Münchenstein, Muttenz, Novartis (long-term partner), Basellandschaftliche Kantonalbank, Habasit, Jenzer Fleisch + Feinkost and a hotel, per the site's logo strip.
w: Novartis paid $678M in July 2020 to settle US claims that it bribed doctors through speaker programmes. No protest at the Kunsthaus found.

f: CHF 30M budget. Basel-Stadt and Riehen give about 9%; the Beyeler Foundation covers a 27% deficit. Sponsors include UBS (Artist Talks) and Globus.
w: UBS paid a $100M US Federal Reserve fine in 2004 for dollar trading with Iran and other sanctioned countries.

f: 2024 income CHF 684k: Stadt St.Gallen 208k, Kanton 196k, other grants 165k (Swisslos, Pro Helvetia, foundations), members and Club der 20 CHF 105k. Raiffeisen funds education.
w: Club der 20 members include UBS and Helvetia; Julius Bär and Würth are firm friends at CHF 500 to 1,500. Swisslos is a public lottery.

f: Funded by members and patrons, City of Zürich and Canton Zürich subsidies, the Ernst Göhner, Foksal Gallery, Gubler Hablützel and Luma foundations, and Ringier AG.
w: Swiss Re and Bloomberg, named in the old note, are not on the 2025 supporter list. No controversy found among the funders listed.

f: Institution of the Migros-Kulturprozent, carried by the Migros cooperative federation, which pays a turnover-based sum into culture since 1957. The sheet lists CHF 12 tickets and no public funder.
w: Migros owns fuel supplier Migrol: CHF 1.3bn of CHF 31.9bn group sales in 2025, about 4%. Fuel is not its main line.

f: Kaohsiung City administrative corporation since 2017; 2025 donors: Applied Materials Taiwan, Rotary 3510, art foundations, shipping, King's Town Bank foundation.
w: Allowed money to name: Applied Materials Taiwan, King's Town Bank charity foundation, Fulong shipping. Only row: 2024 sketching ban.

f: Ju Ming Culture and Education Foundation (net assets NT$446M). 2023 revenue NT$210M: donations 63%, services 22%, shop 10%, grants 5% (Ministry of Culture NT$8.85M for 2023-24).
w: The report names 13 small firms and 68 individual donors, none flagged. NT$132M of donations is not itemised.

n: National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts
f: Funded by the Ministry of Culture. 2025 gifts of NT$5.64M came from property and building-materials firms, the E.SUN Foundation (bank), France's CCAC and individuals.
w: Some donor names are masked in the filing. In Aug 2026 the Gwangju Biennale renamed its Taiwan Pavilion 'NTMoFA', a row not of the museum's making.

f: Founder Chiu Tsai-hsing's private money through Chew's Culture Foundation. No admission fee; running cost about NT$14M a year (2006). No outside sponsors are named.
w: Chiu's money is from electronics firms, among them Jiye Enterprise. The 2006 Global Views article is the latest funding account found.

f: Owned by Taipei City, run by the Taipei Culture Foundation since 2008. Sponsors: Epson Taiwan, Lord Hotels, Contemporary Art Foundation, Sony, Thermos; five more logos unnamed.
w: In 2020-21 director Lo Li-chen cancelled Jun Yang's show, then it was shortened after he threatened legal action. Taipei Times did not call it censorship.

f: Artist-run space founded 2010. In 2013 its director said most money came from sales of donated artworks, plus a small government subsidy (about 15%). No current funder list found.
w: JUT Land Development gave the building 2009 to 2012. The centre's own site fails its certificate check; no 2025 or 2026 programme found.

f: Taipei City agency; 2025-26 sponsors incl. CTBC Culture & Education Fdn (bank), Chanel, Friends of TFAM, Winsing Arts Fdn, Luce Fdn.
w: Dec 2021: Venice pavilion paused over Sakuliu assault claims; victim's lawyer said TFAM's name was used to pressure her. No sponsor row.

f: Ministry of Culture, through its Taiwan Living Arts Foundation. The phase 2 plan (2022-25) totals NT$1.02B, with NT$269M set for 2025. No private sponsors are listed.
w: Run by a foundation under the Ministry of Culture. In 2021 the Executive Yuan cut its public-works plan to about a third.

f: BAB Foundation, chaired by ThaiBev CEO Thapana Sirivadhanabhakdi; ThaiBev is main partner, with Siam Piwat and Central Group (2018). Venice 2026 show adds Bangkok city, TAT, BEM, Ch. Karnchang, Generali.
w: Alcohol money (ThaiBev, Fraser and Neave, SABECO) is no flag. Bangkok city, a partner, censored a July 2025 BACC show, not the biennale.

f: Run by the James H.W. Thompson Foundation, which says it relies entirely on its own funding. The page names its trustees and no outside donors or sponsors.
w: The foundation also supervises the Jim Thompson House Museum. The claim that house-museum income pays for the centre is not on its page.

f: Privately held by the Beurdeley-Bunnag family: Jean Michel Beurdeley, the late Patsri Bunnag and son Eric Bunnag Booth. Shows the family collection; no sponsors or public funders are named.
w: Converted warehouse in Chiang Mai, opened 2016. Admission was planned at about 150 baht. No censorship or protest found.

f: Organised by the Ministry of Culture's Office of Contemporary Art and Culture with Phuket's provincial government, which budgeted THB 59M for 2025-26. Foundations co-fund commissions; none are named.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. 2018 Krabi edition: its organiser, the state OCAC, excluded Chulayarnnon Siriphol's film Birth of Golden Snail unless he cut it.
x: Records
Could not check: the biennale site returned 403 and 429 blocks, so nothing was confirmed beyond its government organisers.

f: Togolese state paid the XOF 2.2bn renovation and funds operations. Director Sonia Lawson sought sponsors in 2019. CFAO and Toyota Tsusho hosted an award show in June 2026.
w: No current budget or sponsor list is published. No censorship, cancelled show or protest found.

c: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
f: Mellon Foundation USD 150,000 over 36 months (awarded February 2024). Nordic Culture Fund and OCA support residencies; co-rd Ltd and Basso Leonard Architects are listed supporters.
w: Artist-run space in Belmont, Port of Spain, 20 years old in 2026. Trinbagonians for Palestine supported a 2025 screening.

f: Run by the Kamel Lazaar Foundation, set up in 2005 by Swicorp founder Kamel Lazaar, a Riyadh-based investment banker. B7L9 opened in 2019 as its first permanent venue.
w: The foundation page names no outside funders. Lazaar once sat on the board of Creative Energy Resources, a power-sector holding. No controversy found.

f: Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation. 2025 income TL 369M, 94% donations; the report says the founders' gifts sustain the museum. Chair İpek Kıraç, a founder, sits on Koç Holding's board.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Arms and defence. Koç Holding owns Tüpraş (oil refining) and Otokar (military vehicles). The report text does not name Koç Holding as a donor.
x: Records
The Suna and Inan Kirac Foundation posts a 2025 activity report and names its six-member board; no donor list or audited accounts found.

f: Founded in 2011 by Garanti BBVA (bank), which runs it as a social investment programme. Garanti executive Ebru Taşcı Firuzbay sits on SALT's board. Entry is free.
w: Global Energy Monitor lists Garanti coal-plant loans (2017 sources). In 2023 350 Turkey asked it at its AGM about financing coal-linked firms.

f: Self-funded by founder Smita Prabhakar, who directs AMS International, a Dubai HR and events firm. Based at Alserkal Avenue; Abdelmonem Alserkal is honorary chairman of the trustees.
w: The National (2024): 'completely self-funded'. A 2017 profile also lists her at Lazer Capital (infrastructure, oil and gas); no source links it to Ishara.

f: Privately funded by Art Jameel, the cultural arm of the Saudi group Abdul Latif Jameel. Not financed or run by the UAE state. No outside sponsors named on its site.
w: Opened November 2018. Abdul Latif Jameel won a 2005 libel appeal against the Wall Street Journal Europe. No protest or censorship found.

f: Creative Scotland, Heritage Lottery Fund, Angus Council, Scottish Government (£5.5M Tay Cities Deal); trusts include Foyle, Robertson, Garfield Weston, William Grant Foundation, Pilgrim Trust, Historic Environment Scotland.
w: Robertson Trust and William Grant Foundation are whisky-endowed; alcohol is not a flag category. No protest found.

f: £3.9M income (FY2025). Arts Council England, Durham County Council, National Lottery Heritage Fund £250k, Wolfson Foundation, Swire Charitable Trust, Art Fund, about 20 other trusts; Darlington Building Society, Global Radio.
w: Arms and Armour Heritage Trust is a heritage charity, not an arms maker. No flagged funder or protest found.

f: Public funders are the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Community Fund. Trusts include Garfield Weston, AKO, Clore Duffield and the Blavatnik Family Foundation; Bloomberg Philanthropies backed the website.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Len Blavatnik's fortune includes the TNK-BP oil venture (Bellingcat, 2019). The map counts such money as fossil-fuel money.
x: Records
Posts trustees' reports and signed accounts for 2016 to 2024, names its eleven directors and keeps a named supporters list with no date.
Finances
Calendar 2025 income GBP 3.73M: about 64 percent gifts and legacies, mostly one 1.55M Schroder donation, 24 percent earned; public funding is not separated in the accounts (SOFA p. 14).

Critique

T. J. Demos, Accumulation (from The Great Transition: The Arts and Radical System Change) (e-flux, 2017): Demos argues that oil and gas sponsorship (BP, Total, Eni, Shell) buys cultural institutions public legitimacy and makes them complicit in climate harm. He treats Liberate Tate, BP or Not BP and allied campaigns as a movement that makes museums sites of political action. Hito Steyerl, Duty-Free Art (e-flux, 2015): Steyerl argues that contemporary art screens how war, tax havens and deregulated finance fracture time and space. She calls freeport vaults secret extraterritorial museums, presents a Syrian heritage foundation as regime public relations, and criticises the Louvre's franchising in autocracies. See the What the field says case study.
Records
The Louvre posts activity reports for 2018 to 2025, a named 2025 donor list, and its 19-member board; no separate accounts page was found.

He later bragged about the visit in emails, including one to Eva Dubin. The Musée d'Orsay did not respond to ARTnews and has not confirmed the visit.
Epstein link: Leon Black, documented

Black lent his Van Gogh "Quarry near Saint-Rémy", valued at $60 million in 2016, to the Orsay's 2014 show "Van Gogh/Artaud: Le Suicidé de la Société". The Art Newspaper reports that the Epstein files indicate his Van Goghs were collateral for large bank loans around 2016. Epstein gave Black "extensive financial advice" for fees of at least $158 million, and Black denies wrongdoing and says he knew nothing of Epstein's crimes until 2019.
