w: Public establishment set up in 1980. 2024 revenue was 421.7M XPF. A friends' association, Amis du Musée, supports it.

n: Papua New Guinea National Museum and Art Gallery
f: A state statutory body funded by the PNG government. Australia paid for its 2015–2018 refurbishment, which reopened on 12 Oct 2018.
w: Australia paid for the building in the 1970s and for its pre-APEC refit in 2018. No corporate sponsor was found.

f: Fiji Government grant: F$697,525 operating and F$500,000 capital in 2018/19. US Ambassadors Fund has paid for digitisation since 2021; it runs out in Sept 2026.
w: A statutory body under the Fiji Museum Act. It needs $300,000 more to finish digitising by Dec 2028.

n: Oceania Centre for Arts, Culture and Pacific Studies (USP)
f: A unit of the University of the South Pacific, owned by 12 Pacific governments including Fiji. Its 2026 residency is run with Creative New Zealand and Creative Australia.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Fiji, USP's host and an owner, halted its grant in 2020 and deported the vice-chancellor in 2021. It restored funding after the 2022 election.
x: Records
The centre has no records of its own; parent USP posts annual reports, audited statements for 2005 to 2025 and names its Council.

n: IAIA Museum of Contemporary Native Arts
f: Part of IAIA, a federally chartered college: federal funds cover 75% of operating costs, with a $13.48M appropriation confirmed. Ford Foundation (2020) and Art Bridges (2025) granted the museum funds.
w: Trump's FY2026 budget proposed eliminating IAIA; the Senate funded it anyway.

n: Eiteljorg Museum of American Indians and Western Art
f: 2023 revenue $11.5M; Lilly Endowment leads, plus Capital Group, Fifth Third, PNC, OneAmerica and Citizens Energy Group (gas utility), all on its corporate partners page.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Citizens Energy Group delivers natural gas in Indianapolis. No sponsor withdrawal or protest aimed at the museum found.
x: Records
It posts annual reports from 2019 to 2024 with a 2024 donor list, a financial summary and board; Form 990s are on ProPublica.

f: Small artist-run centre; Canada Council gave $280k over two years (2017-18); also Manitoba Arts Council, Winnipeg Arts Council and Province of Manitoba.
w: Indigenous artist-run centre founded in 1996 in the Exchange District.

f: Small community art centre; core IVAIS support since 1998-99, plus NT Government, Ian Potter Foundation and Cotton On Foundation (retail).
w: Yolŋu community-controlled art centre, founded 1976. A local landowner corporation that earns bauxite royalties gave money in 2017.

f: Small Aboriginal-run trust at Federation Square. Its 2022-23 report lists Creative Victoria, First Peoples-State Relations and City of Melbourne, plus Viva Energy (oral history), Lendlease and ANZ.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Viva Energy, which supplies about a quarter of Australia's fuel under the Shell brand, is a key sponsor. No protest aimed at the Trust found.
x: Records
It posts annual reports from 2008 to 2023 with full financial statements, a partners and sponsors section and the board.

f: Very small First Nations artist-run space; Australian Government Indigenous Languages and Arts, Creative Victoria and Merri-bek Council.
w: First Nations-led gallery in Brunswick, founded in 2011. Hosted the 2014 '18C' protest show against Racial Discrimination Act changes.

n: Sámi Center for Contemporary Art (Sámi Dáiddaguovddáš)
f: Sámi Parliament direct grant of NOK 6.09M in 2025 (NOK 5.88M in 2024), against total operating revenue of NOK 7.92M.
w: Foundation in Karasjok led by Monika Anti. The other NOK 1.8M of 2025 revenue is not itemised in the sources read.

f: Creative New Zealand gives core funding and is the principal funder. Total revenue in 2025 was NZ$1.16M.
w: Māori arts charitable trust founded in 1996. Its 2025 annual report, published June 2026, names Creative New Zealand as principal funder.

f: Small photo museum (193k visitors 2019); City of Amsterdam, tickets, VriendenLoterij, VandenEnde Foundation, Garanti BBVA International (bank), Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation.
w: Roster read via a Dec 2025 archive of its partnerships page; a lottery and a bank are the corporate names to know.

f: City of Winterthur gives CHF 738k a year for 2025-2032; also Canton of Zurich, Verein, Volkart Stiftung, Ringier, Monterosa and about 20 foundations.
w: Name to know: the Krupp foundation, a funder that holds 10% of warship builder TKMS and 21% of thyssenkrupp.

f: €8.6M budget in 2024, 68% from the Ministry of Culture; Jaeger-LeCoultre, CHANEL, Fondation Neuflize OBC, Louis Roederer and Swiss Life also fund it.
w: 2013 censorship row: after a complaint from the CRIF, the culture ministry made it add visitor notices to Ahlam Shibli's show.

f: About $8M revenue and $15M expenses (FY2023 Form 990); corporate supporters are Fondation d'entreprise Hermès, Select Equity, Harlowe, Paramount Global, MPB and Hearst.
w: 2020 open letter from about 150 community members over students' protest photos; ICP refused to make students take them down.

n: ZKM Center for Art and Media
f: About 250k visitors in 2023; the City of Karlsruhe and Baden-Württemberg are founders and split core funding. EnBW is its partner, with BBBank and dm as project sponsors.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. EnBW owns about 84% of gas group VNG and still burns coal. No protest or petition aimed at ZKM or its EnBW tie found.
x: Records
It posts no annual reports or accounts; partners show as logos, and its board of trustees is named as of September 2026.

f: City of Linz and Linz AG, the city's wholly owned utility (core partners); Land Oberösterreich, Siemens, KUKA, Dorotheum, ORF and others as supporting partners.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Linz AG: Sold 819.11 GWh of gas to 27,534 gas customers in 2025. Natural gas fuelled 81.30% of its own electricity generation and 59.12% of its district heat. Bloomberg Philanthropies, a name under campaign in London, is a current project partner. Ars Electronica itself has not been targeted.
x: Records
It posts no annual report; accounts are filed in the Austrian company register, partners show as logos, and an advisory board is named.

f: Private foundation financed by tickets, books, sponsors, donations and its Friends, and funded by the Berlin Senate culture department. Corporate members: DKB, GASAG and Pfizer Deutschland.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. GASAG, Berlin's gas supplier founded in 1847, is a current corporate member. No protest or boycott aimed at C/O Berlin found.
x: Records
It posts no annual report or accounts; sponsors show as logos, and its advisory board is named.

f: Ville de Paris is main partner. Patrons include ADAGP, Fondation BIC, Fondation Hermès and Rubis Mécénat, the endowment fund of fuel and gas distributor Rubis.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Rubis distributes fuels, heating oils, lubricants, liquefied gases and bitumen, and holds a stake in a Caribbean refinery.
x: Records
Its partners page names backers without an overall date; it posts no reports or board, and its register accounts were not checked.

f: Opened 12 Sep 2025 for about US$100M (building and collection); Astana Motors (cars, malls) pays running costs, and Halyk Bank has been Lead Partner since Mar 2026.
w: Private museum of Nurlan Smagulov. Its lead bank partner is majority-owned by Nazarbayev's son-in-law Timur Kulibayev.
x: US embassy cables say Timur Kulibayev, the president's son-in-law, controlled Halyk Bank: a 2005 cable reports a controlling interest; a 2008 note says he and Dinara Kulibayev each own half of Almex, which owns Halyk. The atlas lists Halyk as the museum's lead partner.

f: Produced by the state Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation. Lead partners: Tourism Committee, Chamber of Commerce and Bukhara Oil. Partners include ACWA Power, Agrobank, Uzcard and Yandex Uzbekistan.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. First edition opened 5 September 2025. ACWA Power sponsored the display of the AlMusalla Prize design.
x: Records
Its own site would not open; parent ACDF posts no reports or accounts, and an advisory board was announced publicly.

f: State museum network under the Ministry of Culture, whose minister appointed its management. BP paid for pipeline rescue archaeology in the 2000s (2010 book); no current corporate sponsor found.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In May 2022 ministry-appointed managers fired about 40 staff; sacked curators cite critical posts and a new union.
x: Records
It posts annual reports from 2005 to 2017 only; no accounts, donor names or board were found on its site.

n: Center of Contemporary Art Tbilisi (Tbilisi Triennial)
f: Key benefactors: Peter Moening Foundation, Modern Ancient Brown Foundation, Swiss SDC, ERTOBA Georgia, DVV International, German Foreign Office, Danish Cultural Institute, New Democracy Fund (Denmark), Hastings Audio Network.
w: Lists 100+ international partners and donors. Georgian Dream's grants laws target foreign funding of arts groups (Freemuse, 2026). No action against CCA found.

f: State non-commercial organisation under Armenia's culture ministry, set up by ministry order in 2002. The ministry bought a Gorky work for it. Lincy Foundation helped pay the 2004 renovation.
w: The Lincy Foundation's help with the 2004 renovation is 22 years old; no current corporate sponsor is named in the sources.

f: Opened 20 Mar 2009 with about 800 works; founded by First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva and funded by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, which she heads.
w: A ruling-family foundation is its only known funder; the director since 2012 is Aida Mahmudova, founder of YARAT.
x: WikiLeaks, 2010-01-27

A US Embassy Baku profile says the First Lady's art collection became the base of Baku's new Museum of Modern Art, which "opened quietly last fall". It writes that her family is believed to exert control over the culture ministry.

n: National Museum of the Republic of Kazakhstan
f: A state museum opened in 2014 with about 175,000 objects, run by the Ministry of Culture and Information; its budget is not published and no corporate sponsors are listed.
w: Aug-Sep 2026 show co-organised with sanctioned oligarch Vladimir Potanin's Olympic Collection.

n: State Museum of Arts of Uzbekistan
f: State museum founded in 1918. The state Art and Culture Development Foundation runs a museum renovation programme that includes it. No budget or funder list is published.
w: 2023: RFE/RL reported the museum withheld Vyacheslav Akhunov's 1987 Bukhara painting from a show; it issued no statement. ACDF also runs the Bukhara Biennial.
x: Records
The museum and its renovation sponsor, the Art and Culture Development Foundation, publish no reports, accounts or funder list, and name only a chairperson.

f: University museum of IFAN and Cheikh Anta Diop University. Its partners page lists Senegal's arts and heritage directorates, Fondation TOTAL Sénégal, Fondation SOCOCIM, Fondation Volkswagen and the Goethe-Institut.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels.
x: Records
The museum sits inside IFAN at Cheikh Anta Diop University and posts no reports, accounts, donors or board of its own.

f: About 1.3-1.5bn FCFA executed in 2025 (~US$2.3M), nearly 80% from the Burkina state; EU 195M FCFA, plus the UN, OIF, LONAB lottery and telecoms.
w: Pan-African film festival, held every two years since 1969. The 2025 edition was nearly 80% state-funded under the military transition.

f: Terra Foundation for American Art gave $150,000 (2023) and $100,000 (2025). The 2024 edition also thanked Open Society Foundations, Pro Helvetia, Goethe-Institut, Institut Français and Lagos State.
w: Run by Àkéte Art Foundation. The 5th edition is titled The Museum of Things Unseen.

f: Tiny association with project grants: Fondation Langlois (2001) and EU ACPCultures, EUR 399,409 (2009 award). No funder list for the 2020s found.
w: Own site ker-thiossane.org refuses connections and the Wayback Machine rate-limited; the Partcours profile lists projects, not funders.
x: Records
Its website ker-thiossane.org refused the connection, so nothing could be checked; the Partcours festival page lists festival supporters only.

f: State subsidy of 327M CFA francs a year; tickets cover about a third of costs (AFP, 2021). China National Petroleum funded the oil exhibition, Orano the uranium show.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. CNPC is China's state oil company. Its oil exhibition at the museum includes a large model of the Zinder refinery.
x: Records
No official site was found for this national museum, and nothing from it or its ministry on reports, accounts, donors or board.

f: Founder Vitshois Mwilambwe Bondo says he funds it from his art sales and sponsors, mostly for the Congo Biennale. Works with Fondation Montresso. Sited in the TEXAF concession.
w: He says the Congolese government gives no support. Sponsors are unnamed. Pro Helvetia reported a 2024 artist residency there.
x: Records
No Kin ArtStudio site could be opened; one interview names only Fondation Montresso as partner, and the founder funds it from art sales.

f: Cameroon's culture ministry. AFD gave EUR 1M through a debt-reduction contract from 1 October 2019; Expertise France ran the 2020 to 2024 modernisation.
w: National museum since 1988, in the former presidential palace; it reopened in 2015 after renovation.

f: ACCRA [dot] ALT festival. 2023 supporters: Ghana's tourism and culture ministry, Ghana Tourism Authority, Korle Klottey Municipal Assembly, Ghana Museums and Monuments Board, Citi FM/TV, Institut Français.
w: The organiser's own press release lists the supporters. The 2023 edition moved from James Town to Osu; no reason was given.

f: Small independent non-profit founded 1998 by William Wells, now a foundation; no funder list found and its website no longer resolves.
w: Egypt's first independent contemporary art space; closed after a state raid in 2015, then ran from a converted factory.

f: Cultural association funded by private Tunisian patrons who are not named, per its director. Partner: African Culture Fund. No budget or donor list published.
w: Renovation was handled by Mamia Taktak (director Camille Lévy, 2022). 32bis.org lists no supporters, partners or accounts.
x: Records
32bis.org lists no annual reports, accounts, partners, funders, board or team.

f: State museum. A 2001 World Bank loan (~24M TND, plus 9.5M TND from the state) paid for the 2009-12 expansion; a 2017 Louvre partnership was backed by TOTAL Tunisie, Loukil, ATUGE and Dar El Marsa.
w: Tunisia's largest museum, known for its Roman mosaics; closed July 2021 to Sept 2023.

f: Algerian State. Its 1985 statute makes it a public administrative establishment under the culture minister, funded by State, local and public-body subsidies, gifts and entry fees.
w: State oil firm Sonatrach handed over 174 Guccione paintings in 2012, a one-off gift. The museum site names no sponsor.

f: Private foundation and residency (opened 2009) funded entirely by its founder, the French businessman Jean-Louis Haguenauer; no other sponsors are named.
w: Residency on a 10-hectare olive grove 20 km outside Marrakech, hosting about 40 artists a year; visits by appointment.

f: Run by Fondation Al Mada (formerly Fondation ONA), the corporate foundation of Al Mada, the royal family's holding company; Le360 (2023) confirms it manages the Casablanca and Rabat villas.
w: Al Mada's unit Nareva holds over half of the 1,386 MW Safi coal plant, alongside banking, telecom and wind. No protest aimed at the villa found.

n: Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (MAMM)
f: Mid-size private museum founded 1978; pillars are Medellín city hall, national Culture Ministry, Comfama, SURA, Bancolombia, EPM, Fundación Fraternidad and Fundación MUV.
w: Roster read on its own Pilares y aliados page. Public utility EPM is a pillar; Celsia (an energy firm) is credited for website support.

n: Museo Nacional de Etnografía y Folklore (MUSEF)
f: State museum (60 years in 2022) funded through the Fundación Cultural del Banco Central de Bolivia, a public body under the central bank.
w: Holds more than 33,000 cultural objects. Its director was pushed out in 2020 after a change of government and reinstated in 2021.

f: State national museum; the government has budgeted about US$100M for a new building, with a state-owned enterprise managing construction.
w: The government overturned the jury's choice of design for the new building in July 2026.

f: Ministry of Culture museum with a 2021 budget of about COLONES 1.77bn (about US$3M), 48% of it salaries; about 37,000 visitors in 2018.
w: Public collection museum in La Sabana. Its board approved lending works to the presidential offices in Sep 2026 without saying which works.

n: Museo Nacional de Arte Moderno Carlos Mérida (MUNAM)
f: State museum of the Ministerio de Cultura y Deportes, which spent over Q16M (about US$2M) on roof and museography works in 2023-25.
w: Closed since Nov 2022, with no reopening date as of Oct 2025.

n: Fundación Casa de los Tres Mundos
f: Small cultural foundation built with German, Austrian, Swiss and Dutch government grants and the City of Granada; closed by the Nicaraguan state in 2024.
w: Founded 1987-89 by Ernesto Cardenal and Dietmar Schönherr. Ran art and music schools and Radio Volcán.

f: Corporate sponsorship programme for its eight rooms. Pillar companies on its site: Pollo Campero, Pepsi and CMI, from the 2019 roster. Part of Universidad Francisco Marroquín.
w: The sponsors page still shows the 2019 roster. OpenSanctions has no match for CMI, Pollo Campero or Dionisio Gutiérrez.

f: Privately owned museum founded in 1926; a foundation was set up in 1959 to maintain it. No funder list, annual report or accounts found.
w: Pre-Columbian collection of about 45,000 objects. Led by president and CEO Andrés Álvarez Calderón Larco.
x: Records
Larco publishes no annual reports, accounts or sponsors; its directory names only an executive president and a director, not a board.

f: A small state-backed museum: most of its money comes from Finland's Ministry of Education and Culture, plus a yearly grant from Inari Municipality.
w: Owned by the Sámi Museum Foundation, whose board must be at least half Sámi. Its exhibition renewal was paid for by Finnish foundations.

f: 2023: about NOK 15M in public operating grants, NOK 13.1M of it from the Sámi Parliament (Sametinget), plus Finnmark county and four municipalities.
w: A Sámi museum foundation running several sites. It had 14,467 visitors in 2023 and has no corporate sponsors.

f: About NOK 32M a year (2022). 96% is public grants and the rest comes from non-profit foundations; it has no commercial sponsors.
w: The regional art museum for Northern Norway, with a strong Sámi programme. It opened a Bodø venue in 2025 and programmes Nordover in Longyearbyen.

f: 2023 revenue US$21.5M (IRS 990), from state and federal agencies, Hawai'i foundations such as Kamehameha Schools, and Hawai'i corporate sponsors.
w: Hawai'i's state museum of natural and cultural history, founded in memory of Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop.

n: Greenland National Museum and Archives (Nunatta Katersugaasivia Allagaateqarfialu)
f: DKK 13.6M operating grant from Greenland's 2024 budget. Augustinus Fonden gave DKK 4.5M for a 2025-27 research project and funds two others. Beckett-Fonden also gave.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden's investment arm holds over 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
x: Records
It posts activity reports from 2001 to 2024 without accounts; its site names managers and no board or donors.

n: Listasavn Føroya (National Gallery of the Faroe Islands)
f: Public grants from the Faroese parliament and government. Augustinus Fonden gave DKK 17M in 2022 for building development, after co-funding the 1993 extension with Tórshavn, Fossbankin and Danish foundations.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden owns Chr. Augustinus Fabrikker, which holds over 25% of cigar and pipe-tobacco maker Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
x: Records
It posts no reports, accounts or donor list, says it runs on public funds, and names four board members.

f: Vanuatu statutory body. Its 2025 newsletter lists government grants, international donors, corporate sponsors and museum income, all unnamed. UNESCO's Heritage Emergency Fund paid for post-quake repairs to May 2026.
w: The fund's donors include the Qatar Fund for Development, Norway, Canada, the UK and France. Online fundraising followed the Dec 2024 quake.

f: Solomon Islands Government (department of the Ministry of Culture and Tourism). Its 2024 virtual museum was funded by Australia's Digital Pasifik project, with British High Commission support.
w: Virtual museum launched Oct 2024 with both national libraries of Australia and New Zealand; the museum now owns and sustains the site.

f: Small foundation-run house (2025); carried by the Christoph Merian Stiftung, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft and the Federal Office of Culture.
w: Building is at Freilager-Platz 9 in Münchenstein. Education is funded by Göhner and Binding; the Pax Art Awards by Art Foundation Pax, an insurer's foundation.

f: Small art-and-tech centre (2025) with structural funding from Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles, Flanders and VGC, plus the National Lottery and the ERDF.
w: Canal-side centre and fablab in Molenbeek. Its private partners are Fondation Orange (telecom) and Selligent (software).

n: V2_ Lab for the Unstable Media
f: Small foundation (2025–2028 plan) with structural funding from the Creative Industries Fund NL and the City of Rotterdam, plus EU project grants.
w: Founded 1981. Dutch arts cuts after 2012 forced a reorganisation and ended DEAF, last held in 2014.

f: Slovenian Ministry of Culture and City of Ljubljana, plus European Commission programmes (Creative Europe, Horizon 2020, ERDF, Interreg) and the Swiss Contribution, per the institute's supporters list.
w: Kersnikova Institute runs Kapelica Gallery, the Rampa Lab and BioTehna. Slovenia's culture portal lists it as an EU Creative Europe funding recipient.

f: Corporate cultural facility (2026) run and paid for by NTT East, a telecom operator, in Tokyo Opera City Tower.
w: Opened in 1997 to mark the centenary of Japan's telephone service. A non-profit art and science venue, not a commercial attraction.

f: Annual festival (2026) funded since 2004 by the Kulturstiftung des Bundes. Berlin Senate, bpb, Medienboard and Creative Europe funding was listed for 2020–21.
w: Coordinates mark central Berlin, because festival venues change each year. Its 2026 partner programmes include the Schering Stiftung and HAU.

n: LABoral Centro de Arte y Creación Industrial
f: Public foundation (budget about €1.3M in 2014) governed by Asturias, Gijón city and the Gijón Port Authority. Project sponsors in 2023 included the Onassis Foundation's Ariona Hellas.
w: Housed in the Universidad Laboral building. Fundación EDP, an energy group's foundation, co-funded the Eco-Visionarios exhibition in 2018–19.

f: Small nonprofit (revenue $1.63M in 2023), funded by Atlantic, Ford, Jerome and Arison Arts foundations, the NEA, NYSCA and NYC DCLA.
w: Art-and-technology nonprofit registered in Brooklyn as Eyebeam Atelier Inc. Arison Arts Foundation is Arison-family money.

f: Smithsonian federal base plus donors, October 2023 to September 2024: Adobe, Luce Foundation and NYC Cultural Affairs at $100k+. Bloomberg Philanthropies, Apple and PwC gave $25-49k.
w: Name to know: Bloomberg Philanthropies, which 260 UK artists asked five London theatres to drop in May 2026; not targeted here.
x: Democracy Now!, 2025-08-13

Democracy Now!, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported a White House plan for a far-reaching review of Smithsonian exhibitions to align them with Trump's interpretation of U.S. history. It followed the removal of references to his impeachments.

f: 2023: about two-thirds own earnings and under one-third state grant; Danish foundations pay for buildings and shows, Augustinus Fonden among them.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Augustinus Fonden, which part-owns Scandinavian Tobacco Group, funds its buildings and shows.
x: Records
It posts Danish annual reports from 2012 to 2025 with an income and expense account, names its funders for 2025 and lists its board.

f: 2024: EUR 16.1M income, EUR 11.7M of it federal base funding; sponsors Porsche Holding Salzburg, Wienerberger, Wiener Städtische, Swarovski and others.
w: Porsche Holding Salzburg, a VW Group firm, began a multi-year partnership in 2024; 174,476 visitors in 2024.

f: 2025-26: private foundation subsidised by Vitra AG; show sponsors include Maharam, Camper and IKEA Stiftung, plus the Design Circle friends.
w: Independent foundation set up by Vitra and Rolf Fehlbaum in 1989; furniture-company money throughout.

f: 2023: US$42.5M revenue, US$25.1M of it contributions; founder Corning Incorporated is the main funder, with New York State grants.
w: Founded 1951 by Corning Glass Works; budget is large but attendance (about 400k, 2012) is under the 500k line.

n: Die Neue Sammlung - The Design Museum
f: Bavarian state museum under the Bavarian Ministry of Science and the Arts. Its 2025 centenary show was funded by the ministry, PIN. Freunde der Pinakothek der Moderne and Allianz.
w: Allianz's US unit, AGI US, pleaded guilty to securities fraud in 2022 and agreed to pay $5.8bn. PIN. Freunde lists Allianz as partner in 2026.

f: FY2025 income JPY 150.2M: admissions 77.7M, other business income 67.1M (shop, catalogues, fees), member dues 1.8M, donations and grants 3.5M.
w: Public-interest foundation directed by Naoto Fukasawa. Founded 1936 with backing from industrialist Magosaburo Ohara. No donor roster published.

f: 2025: city-run (committee chaired by Cheongju's mayor) with national Korea Art Festival support; partners Hyundai Motor, Genesis, Hyundai Department Store, Aero K, Emart24.
w: Flags: Forced or exploited labour. Hyundai Motor, a 2025 partner: its subsidiary SMART Alabama hired children as young as 12 (Reuters, 2022). Over 400,000 visitors in 2025.
x: Records
Its site failed a certificate check; searches found only press coverage of the organizing committee, no reports, accounts, donors or board.

f: About EUR 5.2M income in 2024, mostly Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science money, with Ammodo as main partner, plus Rabobank and De Nederlandsche Bank.
w: Main partner Ammodo (2022-26). Brouwerij 't IJ (alcohol) backs Open Studios. A Dec 2024 alumni campaign challenged its governance.

f: Institutional funding comes from the Berlin Senate Department for Culture, cut by about EUR 149k in 2025; national arts councils and KfW Stiftung fund residencies.
w: Residency house founded 1974. About 30 foreign arts councils and ministries pay for its studio places.

f: A public-law foundation run and financed by the state of Baden-Württemberg; programme partners include KfW Stiftung and Robert Bosch GmbH.
w: State-founded residency (1990) in a baroque palace. It runs a code of conduct for fellows, introduced after an Oct 2023 open letter.

f: A public-benefit foundation funded by France's Ministry of Culture, the City of Paris and the Académie des Beaux-Arts, plus about 135 partners who rent studios.
w: 310 live-in studios in the Marais and Montmartre. Corporate patrons are Samsung Foundation of Culture, Icatu and Neuflize OBC.

n: Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity
f: Alberta public institution. In 2022-23 Suncor Energy Foundation gave C$1M-4.9M and Shell Canada C$100k-250k; lifetime donors include Cenovus, BP Canada and Chevron Canada. RBC, BMO and TD also give.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Suncor Energy Foundation sits in the C$10M+ lifetime tier. The 2022-23 list is the latest published.
x: Records
It posts annual reports for 2013-14 to 2025-26 with audited statements attached, names donors by year through 2022-23, and lists its 11 governors.

f: 2025-26: Canada Council, BC Arts Council, Province of BC and City of Vancouver, with the Audain Foundation and Western Front Foundation at $20k+.
w: Artist-run centre founded in 1973 by eight artists. Its building was bought in 2015 with C$1.5M of developer Rize's city amenity money.

f: Private donors in 2025. Underwriters: Bloomberg Philanthropies, Eleanor Acquavella, Marina Kellen French Foundation. Benefactors include Blavatnik Family Foundation and Pollock-Krasner Foundation. 2023 expenses about $4.1M.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Blavatnik Family Foundation money comes from Len Blavatnik's oil fortune (TNK-BP), per Bellingcat (2019). Bloomberg Philanthropies underwrites; UK artists asked five London theatres to drop it in 2026, not Skowhegan. Blavatnik also gives, and his Oxford gifts drew criticism.
x: Records
Only the 2025 annual report is online, with donors named by giving level; Form 990s are on ProPublica and trustees and governors are listed.

f: Creative Scotland (29% of annual costs per its support page; £133,000 in FY2025), £286,294 Culture Collective award 2026. Trusts: Hugh Fraser, Garfield Weston, Foyle, Kone, Leche; Argyll and Bute Council.
w: Founded 1999 by Eileen and Peter Jacobs. Other funders include Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, French ministries, British Council and the Swedish Embassy.

f: Private art school in Manhattan. The Rhodes family owned it until 1 September 2025; the nonprofit SVA Alumni Society owns it now. No sponsor list found.
w: Flags: Epstein-linked, Protest or boycott. Chair David Ross resigned in February 2026 after his Epstein emails surfaced. Students held a May 2024 sit-in demanding SVA divest from Israeli weapons makers. See the Epstein cross-reference.
x: Epstein link: David A. Ross, documented

Ross, a former director of the Whitney, SFMOMA and ICA Boston, stayed close friends with Epstein after his 2008 conviction, kept in contact until at least 2016 and says he contacted Epstein again in 2019. SVA accepted his resignation, effective 3 February 2026, after a student petition.
Records
sva.edu posts no annual report, financial statements or donor list but names its 10-person board of trustees; no filings under the school's own name.

Critique

Kuba Szreder, Productive Withdrawals: Art Strikes, Art Worlds, and Art as a Practice of Freedom (e-flux, 2017): Szreder argues that art strikes, boycotts and occupations are productive withdrawals that generate collective creativity and new commons-based institutions. He surveys the 2014 boycotts of Manifesta, the São Paulo and Sydney biennials, Poland's art workers' strike and Gulf Labor actions at the Guggenheim. Ghalya Saadawi, Post–Sharjah Biennial 10: Institutional Grease and Institutional Critique (e-flux, 2011): Saadawi argues that the fallout from Sharjah Biennial 10 should widen into a critique of how institutions and capital shape art, beyond boycotts alone. She questions the Sharjah Art Foundation's conduct and state funding, and the Guggenheim's censorship of Hans Haacke in 1971. See the What the field says case study.
