f: Founded 1996 as Ukraine's first gallery with municipal status. The city council culture department decides on its premises. No budget, sponsor list or donor list is published.
w: Upper halls closed since 2022 and its White Cube now serves the city's news studio. The ARTbasement, also a shelter, reopened in September 2023.
x: Records
The gallery's site returned HTTP 403, so nothing could be checked; it is a city council institution.

f: Founding partners: Edo State Government, Germany's Foreign Office, Mellon Foundation, British Museum, PI Trust. Leadership Circle donors include NNPC Seplat Energy, Lekoil Nigeria and Azura Power West Africa.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. Oba loyalists disrupted the 9 November 2025 preview. Edo's Assembly urged a state takeover on 22 December 2025.
x: Records
It names donors by tier (undated) and eight trustees, but posts no annual report or accounts.

f: State enterprise. 2025: UAH 38.0M state budget, UAH 24.2M own income. Project partners include Erste Foundation, British Council, the US Embassy and International Renaissance Foundation.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott, State censorship or punishment. In July 2013 the director had Volodymyr Kuznetsov's painting painted black and Vasyl Tsagolov's work excluded; artists called a boycott. 2025 visitors: 53,870.
x: Records
It posts annual reports for 2017 to 2025 and audited statements for 2014 to 2019; the 2025 report names partners; no board is listed.

f: State museum. The Cabinet gave it UAH 5.6M in 2020 for emergency facade repairs. Donations go to its own charitable foundation. No corporate sponsor list is published.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In October 2012 staff sent an open letter demanding the removal of acting director Tatiana Mironova; art workers backed it with a statement and petition.
x: Records
Its public information page holds a 2021 budget and utility compliance notes only; no annual report, accounts, donor list or board.

f: Fundación Malba, set up by Eduardo Costantini, covers the annual deficit; own income pays about half the budget. Collaborators on its sponsors page include Chevron, Bloomberg, Zurich and Telecom.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Chevron is a listed collaborator. Costantini's ex-wife said in August 2026 she will sue over founding-collection works; MALBA says its foundation owns them.
x: Records
It posts financial statements for 2005 to 2024 but no annual report; sponsors show only as logos and no board members are named.

n: Museo de la Solidaridad Salvador Allende
f: Servicio Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural grant of CLP 660M in 2025. Project money from Fondart, the Senate, Henry Moore Foundation and Centro Cultural de España. Metro is a media partner.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In 2023 Allende's grandson wrote to the museum, then campaigned publicly, demanding Tania Bruguera's show be cancelled. It opened late and modified.
x: Records
It posts annual reports for 2014 to 2025, balances, a 2025 list of funders and agreements, and five named directors.

n: Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico
f: Private nonprofit. Current exhibitions are backed by the Flamboyan Foundation, Mellon Foundation, Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, Mano Amiga and the Puerto Rico Tourism Company. No corporate donors are named.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. On 19 November 2023 activists picketed after the Cecilia Orta Allende gallery was renamed for a donor family tied to the Fiscal Oversight Board.
x: Records
Its site names 19 board members but posts no annual report, accounts or donor list; Form 990s for 2000 to 2025 are on ProPublica.

f: Run by National Museums of Kenya, a state corporation. The Planet Africa project (opened November 2024) lists the German Research Foundation and Germany's Foreign Office as funders. No sponsor list.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In May 2017 museum management pulled works by Michael Soi, Patrick Mukabi and Bertiers Mbatia on opening day, saying they were unsuitable for children.
x: Records
No records of its own: parent National Museums of Kenya posts annual reports for 2015 to 2019 and names its board; no accounts or donors.

n: National Museum of Fine Arts of Chile (MNBA)
f: State museum under the Servicio Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural; buys works from its own budget. Gifts came through Fundación AMA from collector Juan Yarur Torres and from artist Cecilia Vicuña.
w: 510,720 visitors in 2024, a decade high. Cancelled a León Ferrari retrospective in June 2026, citing budget cuts. Not the Buenos Aires museum.

f: Municipal foundation. The City of Cuenca gives about $500,000 per edition. The foundation's 2023 report names agreement partners: Prefectura del Azuay, Universidad de Cuenca, Plásticos Rival, Spanish and Italian embassies.
w: In November 2025 a private group, DPOT, threatened the biennial over one work. It filed a complaint and kept the work on view.

f: Founded by musician X Alfonso. In 2014 the Cuban Music Institute and Ministry of Culture covered some costs until it became self-financing. It occupies a state-owned building.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. The ministry's music centre cancelled a Celia Cruz tribute there in October 2025. It closed temporarily in June 2026; Prensa Latina blames the US embargo.
x: Records
Its site offers two dossiers and nothing else: no annual report, accounts, sponsor list or board.

f: Organised by Yayasan Biennale Yogyakarta, a state-funded foundation created in 2010. The Yogyakarta regional government ran the 2019 edition. No corporate sponsors found.
w: On 9 October 2026 it announced closure after 16 years, citing rising censorship and violence against activists. It names no incident against itself.

f: Run since 2024 by Majelis Jakarta, an artist-collective network. 2026 partners: Dulux, Artotel's Paviliun Raden Saleh, iForte. Jakarta culture office and Jakpro logos are unlabelled; no budget published.
w: Founded 1974 by the Jakarta Arts Council. The 2026 edition, KEBAL, runs 4 Oct to 28 Nov at Taman Ismail Marzuki.
x: Records
The partner page shows sponsor and media-partner logos with role labels only; no reports, accounts, dates or board are published.

f: Run privately by Ayala Foundation, the Ayala group's foundation. Ayala Corporation co-presents shows; BPI is a partner. The Spanish and US embassies supported the 2024 Zóbel show.
w: Opened 1967 from Fernando Zobel's plan. It closed in 2019 for rebuilding and reopened 4 December 2021. It had 65,000 visitors in 2014.

f: Private museum founded in 2010 to show the collection of physician and patron Dr. Joven Cuanang. Run by the non-profit Silangan Foundation; entry is ticketed. No corporate sponsors are listed.
w: Complex designed by artist Antonio Leaño. Ex-curator Riel Hilario criticised its treatment of artists and 50% commission in April 2021; it issued no statement.

f: Privately owned by DTAC telecom founder Boonchai Bencharongkul, who built it in 2012 for his collection of over 1,000 works. His son Kanachai runs it; tickets cost THB 250.
w: Also runs the ART Space at Four Seasons Hotel Bangkok, with works on loan from the museum. No sponsors or public grants are listed.

f: Part of PETRONAS, Malaysia's state oil and gas company, which has built the PETRONAS Art Collection since 1993. Nearly two million visitors since 1992.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Left Suria KLCC in July 2026. A preview opened at Ombak KLCC on 21 August 2026; full opening is due by end 2027.
x: Records
No records of its own: owner PETRONAS posts annual and integrated reports for 2014 to 2025, financial reports, and names its eight directors.

f: Administrative corporation. 2025 revenue NT$201M: Tainan City subsidy NT$89.7M, Ministry of Culture and others NT$25M, tickets and parking NT$57M, donations NT$3.7M.
w: Opened 27 January 2019. In 2025 the Ministry of Culture set up a preparatory office for a planned Tainan National Art Museum.

f: Private museum built by collectors Yan Shijie and Cao Mei, who invested nearly RMB 400 million over eight years. It opened in May 2014; no sponsors are listed.
w: The 20,000 sq m site was designed by Dong Yugan of Peking University. Yan is described only as a collector and entrepreneur.

f: Non-profit artist-initiated space founded in 2007. In 2014 it reported no financial support inside Vietnam and relied on unnamed international donors and a benefit auction.
w: In 2016 it closed its residency programme after three exhibitions were cancelled and the Cultural Police issued a warning. The state does not fund it.
x: Records
san-art.org has an expired certificate and was not opened; 2014 to 2018 coverage names a board chair but no annual report.

f: Founded 2018 by ruangrupa, Serrum and Grafis Huru Hara. Own income covered about 30 percent of costs in 2019; their businesses paid the rest. Donor agencies are unnamed.
w: Name to know: co-founder ruangrupa curated documenta fifteen (2022), which drew antisemitism accusations. Ruangrupa and the mural's artists apologised for the stereotypes in it.

f: State gallery owned by Indonesia's Culture Ministry, a ministry created under President Prabowo; before that it sat under the education and culture ministry. Holds 1,770 artworks.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. On 19 December 2024 it cancelled Yos Suprapto's show ten minutes before opening after he refused to cover more paintings of Jokowi.
x: Records
Its site could not be reached, so reports, accounts, funders and board were not checked; no gallery report turned up in search.

f: Not-for-profit museum accredited by Beijing, funded by its gala, patrons, corporate sponsors and grants. 2025 partners: Louis Vuitton, Dior, Bloomberg and Aranya; 901,435 visitors.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. UCCA cancelled a 2019 Hung Liu show after Beijing denied a permit. In 2022 it pulled a Li Songsong painting after a complaint.
x: Records
It posts annual reports for 2024 and 2025, whose 2025 report names partners, and lists about 30 Foundation Council members; no accounts found.

f: Run and paid for by the state-owned West Bund Group. The Centre Pompidou partnership was renewed in 2023 for five years. Joint shows since 2019 drew over 2 million visitors.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Local officials had fewer than five works removed from the 2019 opening show, The Shape of Time. Pompidou says it does not self-censor.
x: Records
Its site could not be reached, so nothing was checked; the state-owned West Bund Group funds it under a five-year Pompidou partnership.

f: Owned by the Government of Malaysia and run by the National Visual Art Development Board, a statutory body under the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture. Most exhibitions are free.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. In February 2020 it removed four works from Ahmad Fuad Osman's retrospective. Nearly 400 artists and 55 collectors petitioned; a deputy minister sought their return.
x: Records
Its site names past main sponsors such as Shell and Petronas on an undated page; reports, accounts and board could not be checked.

f: State museum funded by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. About 1.05 million visitors in 2016. German collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig donated 117 works.
w: Opened in 1963; holds over 110,000 works. Jean Nouvel's larger building was announced in 2014; no budget for either was found.

f: Run by the state-owned Power Station of Art; budget undisclosed and paid mainly from Shanghai city government funds. 2025 partners: Aesop, Denza, Langham hotels and lighting maker Flos.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In 2012 officials demanded cuts to Yuri Albert's work, so he withdrew; a committee rejected Barbad Golshiri's proposal. Both artists published their accounts.
x: Records
The organiser's site renders by script and showed no text, so nothing was checked; the budget is undisclosed and mainly city funds per press.

f: Opened January 2024 by philanthropist Marisa Chearavanont through her Khao Yai Art; no sponsors are named. She is married to Soopakij Chearavanont, chairman of CP Group.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. artn't activists staged a guerrilla protest inside, in shirts reading 'world class exploitation'. CP Group's CP Foods faced 2014 slavery claims in its prawn-feed chain.
x: Records
Its site now redirects to a script-built page that showed only headings, so nothing was checked.

f: Founded by collector and karaoke-club owner Qiao Zhibing, who told The Art Newspaper he paid for it. The government-backed West Bund Group invited him and manages the surrounding park.
w: Opened in March 2019 in five former aviation fuel tanks. Time Out says Qiao invested with West Bund Group; no budget was found.

f: Founding sponsor Eczacıbaşı; main sponsor Doğuş Group with Bilgili Holding. The September 2026 sponsor panel lists Volvo, Visa, Mercedes-Benz, Nescafe, Paribu, TAV Airports and the Istanbul municipality.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. A December 2023 sit-in delivered over 5,500 signatures for full-day free entry and open data. Eight artists and a collective pulled works in 2011.
x: Records
It posts no annual reports or accounts; its sponsor page is one logo panel dated September 2026, and its administration page names the board.

f: State-funded foundation; 2024 income NOK 1,059M, gifts NOK 12.5M. Fredriksen Family Art Company lends its collection on a ten-year deal and funds four PhDs. AKO Foundation and Sparebankstiftelsen DNB give.
w: Flags: Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. June 2022 appeal urged ending the Fredriksen deal; critics cite Seadrill's 2014 Rosneft contract. The museum sees no reason for review.
x: Records
Annual reports run from 2003 to 2025, accounts are filed in the Norwegian register, partners are named without a date, and the board is listed.

f: Run by İKSV. Koç Holding is main sponsor for 2007 to 2036. Its group includes oil refiner Tüpraş, almost half its revenue, and defence maker Otokar.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Arms and defence, Campaigned name, Protest or boycott. Direnal-Istanbul protested Koç's sponsorship at the 2009 opening. In 2013 protesters wore Koç banners. The 2025 edition drew over 600,000 visitors.
x: Records
Reports run from 2013 to 2025, the 2024 one with income and expense tables; Biennial sponsors are named and the trustees and directors are listed.

f: Corporate museum of Borusan Holding, run by the Borusan Kocabıyık Foundation in the holding's headquarters. Group units: EnBW wind power, steel pipe, Cat machinery, car sales. No outside sponsors.
w: Opened in 2011 during the 12th Istanbul Biennial. Borusan EnBW Enerji runs 725 MW of renewable plants.

f: Non-profit Serendipity Arts Foundation, founded by Hero Enterprise chair Sunil Kant Munjal. 2025 partners include the Goa government, Hero Insurance Broking, Hero Realty, Campa, Milton and foreign cultural institutes.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. On 18 December 2019 the organisers shut two exhibits with CAA and NRC content, citing technical issues. Poets called it political suppression.
x: Records
It posts no reports, accounts or full trustee list; its patrons page names nine patrons undated, and the 2025 festival partners page shows only logos.

n: Dr. Bhau Daji Lad Mumbai City Museum
f: Partnership of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, the Jamnalal Bajaj Foundation and INTACH. The Corporation paid about INR 3 crore for the 2025 repairs. No corporate sponsor is named.
w: Mumbai's oldest museum; it reopened on 8 January 2025 after four years closed.

f: Private museum of the Art & Photography Foundation. Founder Abhishek Poddar gave the collection and his family the land. Building donors include Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, Sunil Munjal, Citi and Tata.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In 2016 artists held a sit-in and a 1,000-signature petition against a state deal giving its parent foundation the Venkatappa Art Gallery.
x: Records
It posts annual reports for 2020-21 to 2025-26 and audited statements from 2014-15, names its trustees, and shows founding patrons only as logos.

f: Private trust founded in 1986, funded entirely by the Bengal Group. Chairman Abul Khair Litu co-founded AB Bank. It runs a fine arts gallery, a music festival and publishing.
w: In July 2024 the Anti-Corruption Commission endorsed a charge sheet against Litu for acquiring about Tk 903 million in assets beyond his income.

f: Non-profit company limited by guarantee. Its 2026 disclosure lists COMO Museum of Art, Khurram Kasim Art Foundation, HUM TV, HBL Art Committee, Kadist, AFIELD and private collectors.
w: Runs residencies and exhibitions in Karachi; over 500 artists have taken part in 25 years.

f: Autonomous body funded by the Union Ministry of Culture, founded in 1954. It runs the National Exhibition, the Triennale-India and seven regional centres. No sponsors are listed.
w: The government took over its management in April 2015, citing irregularities. A 2017 Delhi High Court petition claimed misappropriation of funds.

n: Anadolu Kültür (Depo and Diyarbakır Arts Center)
f: Founded 2002; runs Depo in Istanbul and the Diyarbakır Arts Center. Supporters named: Sigrid Rausing Trust, Civil Rights Defenders, Foundation for Arts Initiatives and Stiftung Mercator. No state money listed.
w: Founder Osman Kavala has been jailed since 2017 and got a life sentence in 2022. Turkey neither funds nor controls the group.

f: The Sindh government holds the palace, which it says it bought in 1993; a trust runs the museum. Entry cost Rs 30 in 2020. No sponsors are named.
w: Opened in September 1999 with Treasures of the Talpurs. In 2021 the Sindh High Court ordered a medical college there; the government appealed.

f: Statutory body under the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, founded in 1974, governed by a minister-led Executive Council. It runs district branches, scholarships and the National Art Gallery. No sponsors listed.
w: The venue for most Dhaka Art Summit editions, which the Samdani foundation produces.

f: Private non-profit founded in 2015 by Hamidreza Pejman, who bought the Argo Factory brewery in 2016. No government money paid for restoration; sponsors have since left.
w: Argo Factory is closed until further notice; the war began on 28 February 2026. Pejman says an unnamed body shut its film series over permits.
x: Records
Argo Factory names three in-kind sponsors on an undated page, and lists staff but no board; no reports or accounts are published.

f: State museum owned by the arts deputy of Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, which OFAC lists as an entity. The state set a 16.5 billion toman renovation budget.
w: Flags: Sanctions, State censorship or punishment. After 1979 the state kept its Western collection in storage. In 2017 the culture minister cancelled its Berlin and Rome loan show.
x: Critique

Nasrin Tabatabai, Seep (artists of The People's Art (Witte de With, 2012): The announcement on e-flux says Tabatabai and Afrassiabi set a British Petroleum archive of Iranian oil operations beside the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art's Western collection, assembled in the 1970s oil boom and stored in cellars after 1979, and treat both as suspended archives. See the What the field says case study.
Records
It posts no reports, accounts, funder list or board; its site only names the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance as the owner.

f: Run as a subordinate office of the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, since its 1954 opening, with centres in Mumbai and Bengaluru. No sponsor is listed.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. In 2000 the Culture Ministry ordered a painting pulled and all the artists withdrew. In 2019 members cut off Amol Palekar's criticism of the ministry.
x: Records
It posts nothing itself; its parent Ministry of Culture publishes annual reports from 2014-15 to 2023-24, with no sponsor list or advisory board named.

f: American Friends of the Israel Museum raised over $450M since 1972. Mandel and Safra foundations each gave $12M in 2009. State and city fund 10 to 12%, per Wikipedia.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In July 2009 PACBI, the Palestinian BDS campaign, urged Yinka Shonibare in an open letter not to guest-curate here. He held a 2010 show.
x: Records
Its website would not load; a search shows a named board page, and the Israeli register lists it as a public benefit company.

f: Paulson Family Foundation gave $15M in 2021 and the Eyal & Marilyn Ofer Family Foundation $5M in 2019. No sponsor list found on its site.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In September 2025 over 50 artists signed an open letter asking two exhibiting artists to cancel their show, citing Gaza. The director rejected cancelling exhibitions.
x: Records
Its annual report link returns an error; it posts no accounts or donor list, and its trustees page names the board, undated.

f: Municipal museum group Haifa Museums. Site logos: Haifa Municipality, Ministry of Culture and Sport, Mizrahi Tefahot bank. Japan's embassy gave NIS 15,620 for a 2025 Tikotin show.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In January 2019 hundreds protested the loaned McJesus sculpture. Minister Regev threatened to defund the museum; a deputy attorney general rebuked her. It was removed.
x: Records
No reports or accounts; the sponsorship page names one 2025 foreign-state donor, the Embassy of Japan, beside logos, and the board of directors is listed.

f: Friends association (2015) funds shows and acquisitions via 1,800 NIS memberships and a 23,000 NIS patron tier. British Friends of the Art Museums of Israel back programmes. No budget published.
w: In 2014 the municipality called on the museum to close Arkadi Zaides's Archive; the New York Review of Books reports the museum refused.
x: Records
The Friends association board is listed with Reut Ferster as chair; the museum publishes no reports, accounts or donor names.

f: Partly funded by Israel's Ministry of Culture and the Tel Aviv Municipality. In 2017 co-director Igal Ezrati put public funds at nearly NIS 900,000, a significant share of its budget.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Police barred two film screenings in 2024, the theatre told the High Court. In 2017 Minister Regev asked the Finance Ministry to cut funding.
x: Records
Its site shows no reports or donors; the public board of 27 is listed, and filings sit in the Israeli nonprofit register.

n: Dar Jacir for Art and Research
f: Kickstarter raised nearly $24,000 in 2017. A.M. Qattan Foundation, Sida-funded, announced a $255,691 grant via the Institute for Palestine Studies in March 2018. AFAC lists three grants.
w: Its owners said Israeli soldiers raided it on 15 May 2021 and took equipment, per Hyperallergic. Emily Jacir and Aline Khoury co-direct it.

n: Al Ma'mal Foundation for Contemporary Art
f: Its Donors page shows 27 logos, undated, including Sida, the EU, Norway's ministry, British Council, Ford Foundation, Open Society and DOEN. No budget or dated donor list is published.
w: Core partner of Qalandiya International since 2012. Latest dated funding found: a $171,153 A.M. Qattan Foundation grant in March 2018, Sida-funded.
x: Records
Al Ma'mal shows donor logos with no dates, publishes no reports or accounts, and names its board of directors and General Assembly.

f: Its site lists funders: Stichting DOEN, Gerda Henkel Stiftung, Culture Resource (Mawred), FfAI, Hillman Family Foundations and UCLA Library. No amounts or annual report are published.
w: Asks donors for multi-year unrestricted funds. Founded 1997 in Beirut. Vartan Avakian chairs the board.

f: Created in 2020 by Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Culture; the culture minister chairs its board. No budget or sponsor list found.
w: Flags: Gulf state body. Runs the Diriyah Contemporary Art Biennale and the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah. The foundation says the first Islamic Arts Biennale drew over 600,000 visitors.
x: Records
Its website returned a block page, so reports, accounts, partners and board could not be checked.

n: Arts AlUla and Desert X AlUla
f: Arts AlUla sits inside the Royal Commission for AlUla, a Saudi government agency overseen by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. US nonprofit Desert Biennial produces Desert X AlUla with it.
w: Flags: Gulf state body, Protest or boycott. Three Desert X board members resigned in October 2019, citing Saudi human rights abuses and the Khashoggi killing. MaddocksBrown Foundation, a donor, withdrew its support.
x: Records
Arts AlUla posts nothing; the Royal Commission has 2023 and 2024 annual reports, and Desert Biennial files Form 990s, names donors and lists a board.

f: Subsidiary of the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation (Misk), a non-profit the Crown Prince founded in 2011. No budget or donor list found on its site.
w: Flags: Gulf state body. Founded December 2017; Ahmed Mater was its director then. Its summer 2026 show at Prince Faisal bin Fahd Arts Hall has over 40 works.
x: Records
The Institute posts no reports or board; its parent Misk Foundation lists annual reports for 2019 to 2024, and no accounts or donors are published.

f: Run by Iraq's tourism and antiquities ministry. The US paid about $9M of the 2011 renovation, per its deputy director. Italy equipped its labs in 2015; France sponsored a show.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In 2009 five Iraqi archaeologists wrote an open letter against a sudden reopening; the minister then removed Amira Edan as State Board of Antiquities head.
x: Records
Its site lists no reports, accounts, donors or board, and the ministry that runs it blocked page fetches.

f: Its parent body, the Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums, partners UNESCO's 2025 project: initial budget $175,000, no donor named. No museum budget is published.
w: Closed 7 December 2024 after the fall of Damascus and reopened 8 January 2025. Wikipedia reports six Roman statues stolen in a November 2025 break-in.
x: Records
The parent Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums publishes no annual reports, accounts, donors or board; it is tied to the Minister of Culture.

f: Manages the al-Sabah Collection, on permanent loan to Kuwait under its National Council for Culture, Arts and Letters. Sponsors: KIPCO, Kuwait Petroleum Corporation and subsidiaries, Kuwait Finance House.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Gulf state body. Founded 1983. The collection holds over 30,000 objects, collected by Sheikh Nasser Sabah al-Ahmed al-Sabah. Sheikha Hussa Sabah Al-Salem Al-Sabah is director general.
x: Records
It posts no reports or accounts; its sponsors page names donors and sponsors without a date, and no board roster is named.

f: State museum set up by Royal Decree 62/2013. The Minister of Heritage and Tourism chairs its Board of Trustees. It lists no sponsors or budget.
w: Flags: Gulf state body. Its site describes it as a legal entity with financial and administrative independence. It shows Oman's heritage from earliest settlement to the present.
x: Records
It posts no reports, accounts or sponsors; its board of trustees page names six members, led by the Minister of Heritage and Tourism.

n: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts
f: Owned by the Royal Society of Fine Arts, a private non-profit founded in 1979. A 2022 event launched a Permanent Patrons wall, names not given. No budget or donor list.
w: Opened 19 February 1980. Its site counts over 3,000 works, Wikipedia over 2,000. The expanded building won the 2007 Aga Khan Award.
x: Records
The gallery names patrons by tier on a partners page, undated, and its trustees on the about page; it publishes no reports or accounts.

f: Founded 2016 by Queen Rania. Its 2025/26 partners page names one strategic partner, Greater Amman Municipality; Sukhtian Foundation backs the 2026 student exhibition. No budget or sponsor list.
w: 2016 sponsors were Al Manaseer Group, Zain, Aramex and Al Markaziya. The 2026 edition runs 2 to 17 October across Amman and Aqaba.
x: Records
ammandesignweek.com returned HTTP 403, so nothing could be checked from its own pages.

f: 2013 annual report names Ford Foundation, Sida, AFAC, Medico International and the European Commission. British Council gave £74,976 in 2022, per the Jewish Chronicle. No current donor list.
w: Staff told Al Jazeera that Israeli forces raided it in December 2023 and arrested two directors. Co-founder Juliano Mer-Khamis was shot dead in 2011.
x: Records
The theatre posts annual reports for 2007 to 2013 and 2020, names donors in the 2013 report, lists its board, and publishes no accounts.

f: Founded 2015 by developer Ovidiu Șandor, who provides the building. The 2025 biennial had main partner Ploom, Japan Tobacco's heated-tobacco brand, plus Banca Transilvania, Catena and Timișoara municipality funding.
w: Flags: Tobacco. Runs the Art Encounters Biennial (2015 to 2025). A museum-standard venue in the former Casa ISHO opens in September 2026 with a Picasso show.
x: Records
It posts no reports, accounts or funder list, only a count of 50 partners; the team page names the president but no board.

f: Romanian Ministry of Culture funds it, including RON 500,000 for 2024 acquisitions. Sponsors include AQUA Carpatica, Greentek Lighting, Crama Oprișor, Molotow, UniCredit Bank and BRD Groupe Société Générale.
w: Opened 2004 inside the Palace of the Parliament. ArtMargins writer Augustin Ioan said in 2008 that Prime Minister Nastase financed it in secret.

f: Sofia Municipality funds yearly acquisitions, resumed in 2007. Partners listed: Ministry of Culture, America for Bulgaria Foundation, Aurubis Bulgaria, Institut français and Goethe-Institut. No budget is published.
w: Founded 1928 as part of Sofia's city museum. Holds more than 23,000 works by Bulgarian artists.

f: Funded by Serbia's Ministry of Culture; the museum publishes the ministry's financial plans for 2023 to 2026. No corporate sponsor list found.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. On 30 January 2020 the government replaced acting director Slobodan Nakarada with Viktor Kiš despite a 2019 open call. Board chair resigned; CIMAM objected.
x: Records
A 2022 report, final accounts for 2020 and 2021, a recent balance sheet and financial plans are posted; no funder list or board is named.

f: State gallery funded by Slovakia's Ministry of Culture. Its 2025 budget of €13.2M was later cut to €9.6M; admission revenue was about €330,700. No corporate sponsor list found.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. Šimkovičová dismissed director Alexandra Kusá in August 2024 and accused her of a conflict of interest, which Kusá denies. Rallies and a 360-signature letter followed.
x: Records
Reports of activity and economy run from 2001 to 2025 and accounts are in the Slovak register; no sponsor list or gallery council is posted.

f: State contributory organisation founded by the Ministry of Culture in 2014 and funded by it. The Kunsthalle said the ministry revoked funding for its 2024 programme on 16 January 2024.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Director Jen Kratochvíl resigned on 15 January 2024. The ministry moved the Kunsthalle under the Slovak National Gallery, citing its programme and efficiency.
x: Records
Its own site posts nothing; the parent Slovak National Gallery posts reports for 2001 to 2025 and files accounts in the Slovak register.

n: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest / Hungarian National Gallery
f: Hungarian state museum. 2026 main and featured sponsors: MVM Group (energy, sells gas), E.ON Energiamegoldások, OTP Bank, MBH Bank, Szerencsejáték Zrt. (state lottery), PPG Trilak, Veolia Energia.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Szerencsejáték also runs Tippmix sports betting; as with Loto-Québec, a state lottery operator is a name to know, not a flag. In April 2026 director László Baán quit the National Cultural Fund committee, writing that many grants did not fit its aims. The minister disputed this.
x: Records
It posts yearly budget reports for 2014 to 2025 and budgets to 2026, names its 2026 sponsors, and lists management but no board.

n: Ars Aevi Museum of Contemporary Art
f: EU gave €4.1M for construction through UNESCO, co-funded by Italy and France per the EEAS; Italy's ministry names Italy, Sarajevo Canton and City. Artists donated about 150 works.
w: Renzo Piano designed the building; works began in 2026. The neighbouring History Museum sought protection in July; officials reported partial facade damage at the start.

f: Skopje's Town Assembly founded it in 1964 from donated art; Poland gave the building design. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism approves its annual programme projects. No sponsors found.
w: Holds over 5,500 works. Director Mira Gaćina, in post since 2017, resigned for personal reasons after six years; Tihomir Topuzovski is acting director.

f: Albanian state museum under the Ministry of Economy, Culture and Innovation, per Wikipedia. No sponsors or budget are published.
w: Holds over 5,000 works. Closed for rebuilding with a new annex since 2021, per Wikipedia; in October 2024 the ministry gave no deadline.

f: Independent non-profit founded 2010 by Adela Demetja. Named supporters: Creative Europe, Allianz Kulturstiftung, Pro Helvetia, Robert Bosch Foundation, European Cultural Foundation, Albania's Ministry of Culture, Municipality of Tirana.
w: No permanent venue from 2018; works with local partners. Runs the Curating with Care programme and the Beyond Matter EU project (2019 to 2023).

f: State museum subordinate to Moldova's Ministry of Culture. Its 2024 report names partners USAID, UNESCO, the Embassy of Japan and tranzit.ro; no corporate sponsors are listed.
w: Holds 39,767 works and had 81,147 visitors in 2024. Its Dadiani wing restoration began in 2004; the second sector opened in September 2021.

f: State-funded museum under Latvia's Ministry of Culture. Its 2025 show Light from Italy was backed by the Italian Embassy, Riga City Council, Rietumu Banka and the ministry.
w: Sponsor Rietumu Banka was fined €5.85M in 2021 for anti-money-laundering failures. The museum runs six Riga sites, including the Riga Bourse and Arsenāls.

n: Riga International Biennial of Contemporary Art (RIBOCA)
f: Private. Founded by Agniya Mirgorodskaya, daughter of Russian fishing businessman Gennady Mirgorodsky. The organisers said funding moved to a US charity, Just A Moment, after 2022. No state funder confirmed.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. Curator Žanete Liekīte campaigned against it; four artists withdrew on 30 June 2023. The organisers suspended the third edition in July 2023.
x: Records
Its website address is now a parked for-sale page, so its reports, accounts, funders and board are unchecked.

f: State gallery supported by the Ministry of Culture, the Senate and the EU-funded National Recovery Plan. General partner Komerční banka; others include J&T Banka, Bohemia Sekt and Czech Television.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. A public call by artists and 23 advisory-board resignations in June 2024 criticised director Knastová. Minister Klempíř dismissed her on 19 March 2026.
x: Records
Annual reports run from 2017 to 2025 and the 2025 report names donors with amounts; no full accounts or board are posted.

f: Run by the Arts Council of Mongolia, an NGO. Backers named: Goethe-Institut (2016, 2022), Asia-Europe Foundation, US Embassy and Xacbank (2016), Taiwan Foundation for Democracy (2022). Later editions name none.
w: The 9th edition ran in May 2024 at the Mongolian National Art Gallery and Red Ger Gallery under the theme Seeing is Believing.

f: No funder, budget or annual report found in the sources opened. Its official site did not load.
w: Established 1934; renamed National Museum of Tajikistan in 2011 and moved into a new building in March 2013 with 22 halls and over 50,000 objects.
x: Records
No museum site loaded; a government portal shows it is a state institution under the president's office, and no reports, accounts or funders appear.

f: Founders built its online school at no cost, per 24.kg (2020). Asia Art Archive is a partner on Mobile Library: Kyrgyzstan, April 2025 to June 2026. No funder list found.
w: Co-founder Bermet Borubaeva also co-founded the TRASH environmental art festival in 2009 and co-curates it.
x: Records
No BiSCA website was found; searches show only Asia Art Archive as a project partner, with no reports, accounts, donor list or board.

f: PDVSA, Venezuela's state oil company, runs the centre as its cultural arm. It still held shows in Caracas in June 2025. PDVSA remains under US blocking sanctions.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Sanctions. General licence 52 (March 2026) permits some PDVSA dealings but leaves it listed. Its Maracaibo branch also runs shows.
x: Records
Its parent PDVSA's website did not load and a search found only a 2010 PDVSA annual report, so its records are unchecked.

n: Lugar de la Memoria, la Tolerancia y la Inclusión Social (LUM)
f: Peru's Ministry of Culture pays the budget (S/ 1.84M in 2023). Small grants came from the Gerda Henkel and Ford foundations and the German, Spanish and French embassies.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. The Culture Ministry removed director Manuel Burga in January 2025 without explanation and barred a Palestinian film in October 2026. Miraflores shut it in 2023.
x: Records
It posts annual memorias for 2022 and 2023, names its funders and its Patronato in the 2023 one, and no accounts are posted.

f: Run by IDG with the City of Rio and Fundação Roberto Marinho. Itaú is strategic sponsor; Shell, Instituto Cultural Vale and Motiva are maintainers; IBM, TAG and Bloomberg also give.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Mining disaster. Shell and Instituto Cultural Vale are named maintainers. Vale's Brumadinho dam collapse killed 270 in 2019. Over 8 million visitors in its first decade.
x: Records
Reports for 2020 to 2022 are in its archive, supporters are named undated, the IDG board is listed, and its accounts page failed to load.

n: Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos
f: Government of Chile, through the national heritage service of the Ministry of Cultures: CLP 2.15 billion in 2024. A private foundation runs it. The 2024 report lists no corporate sponsor.
w: 176,846 visitors in 2024. Deputies voted down its funding in November 2022; the Senate restored it. A 3% cut hit all ministries in 2026.

n: Museo Antropológico y de Arte Contemporáneo (MAAC)
f: Ecuador's Culture vice-ministry (merged into Education in 2025) runs and funds it on a budget above USD 2.5M, and pays the city's Malecón 2000 foundation near USD 500,000 a year.
w: Over 530,000 visits were counted by mid-2022. The state spent USD 451,000 on renovation in 2024 after a dispute with the city over upkeep.

n: Museo de la Palabra y la Imagen (MUPI)
f: Private non-profit. AGIAMONDO and the Ford Foundation backed its 2026 archive move; gifts from citizens, the diaspora and firms repay the annexe mortgage. Its site lists no donors or budget.
w: Founded in 1996 and marking 30 years. Its fund drive 'Un techo para la cultura' pays for the annexe that now holds the archive.

f: Inter-American Development Bank (US$1.3M over three years), Bank of Jamaica, Digicel Foundation, Barita, Gore, National Bakery, PwC, the Clara Lionel Foundation and the Miami Foundation.
w: Runs the Kingston Art District and Artwalk Festival; 118 murals painted. First Caribbean NGO to win a UNESCO-Aschberg grant, July 2026.

f: Mellon Foundation ($230,000, 2019); Andy Warhol Foundation ($100,000 in 2017, $100,000 in 2018, 2026 regrants); Rauschenberg Foundation and Lin-Manuel Miranda ($100,000 each, 2017); Flamboyan Arts Fund (2019).
w: Artist-run space in Old San Juan. After Hurricane Maria it distributed over $400,000 to artists and cultural workers.

f: Annual Government of Barbados grant, plus memberships, gate takings, shop sales, ground rentals and consulting fees. The government appoints five of its 14 council members.
w: Incorporated in 1933 and opened in 1934 in a former British military prison at the Garrison, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

c: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
f: NGC, the state National Gas Company, was title sponsor through 2024. 2026 main sponsors: Ministry of Culture, JB Fernandes Trust, OCM; Massy and ANSA McAL foundations and Methanex also support.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. NGC part-funded 2024 and gave nothing in 2025; its name left the festival title that year. The festival was founded in 2011.
x: Records
Annual reports run from 2020 to 2025, the 2020 one with a percentage financial summary; sponsors are logos dated 2026; the board is listed.

f: Owned and paid for by Fundación Carlos Slim; entry is free at both sites. The museum site names no outside sponsors.
w: Name to know: Carlos Slim. Mexico's regulator ruled América Móvil's units dominant in 2014. His CICSA agreed to repair Metro Line 12 after 26 deaths.

n: Centro Cultural de la República El Cabildo
f: Cultural arm of Paraguay's National Congress, paid from the congressional budget (a G. 1.88 billion extension for a new building in 2025). Entry to the ground-floor rooms is free.
w: Shows mid-20th-century to present Paraguayan art, including Olga Blinder and Livio Abramo. A December 2020 fire hit the newer block; the heritage building was safe.

n: Museo de Arte Moderno de Santo Domingo
f: State museum run by the Dominican Ministry of Culture on the Plaza de la Cultura; its director sits on the ministry's Bienal Nacional commission.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. After a December 2019 protest, artists' open letters in 2020 and 2021 blamed the ministry, the museum and its directors for the Bienal's delays.
x: Records
It posts nothing itself; its parent Ministry of Culture posts annual memorias for 2016 to 2025 and financial statements for 2020 to 2025.

f: 2023 budget 168.8M pesos: federal culture ministry 65.3M, Guanajuato 36M, guest country and state 42M, embassies 10.2M, sponsors 15.4M. Sponsors include Yamaha, Mazda, Megacable, HONOR and the FEMSA group.
w: Name to know: Coca-Cola FEMSA, a named sponsor. Chiapas groups have sought to revoke its water permit since 2017; no campaign targets the festival.

f: Financed by the Patiño foundations: the Bolivian university foundation Simón I. Patiño created in 1931 and the Geneva foundation his heirs set up in 1958. No outside sponsor is listed.
w: Opened 1984; one of three Patiño centres. La Paz bought two neighbouring houses and opened new galleries in 2018; over 35,000 visitors a year.

n: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Caracas
f: Venezuelan public museum, under the state's Fundación Museos Nacionales since 2005, with the Ministry of Culture overseeing it. No private sponsor found.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Chávez dismissed founder Sofía Ímber on air in January 2001. A January 2006 Culture Ministry notice dropped her name from the museum.
x: Records
The museum's site and its parent foundation's site did not load, so its records are unchecked.

f: Public cultural body since 2019 joining the French state, Région Guadeloupe, the Département, Cap Excellence and Pointe-à-Pitre. The Région's then-president launched the €83M building.
w: The regional audit court found serious irregularities in 2023. In April 2024 the financial prosecutor searched the Région's offices over the Mémorial's contracts.

f: Owned and funded by Intesa Sanpaolo through its Progetto Cultura. Four museums in Milan, Naples, Turin and Vicenza drew over 750,000 visitors in 2024. No museum budget is published.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. About 30 Extinction Rebellion activists occupied the Turin site on 2 March 2025 over owner Intesa Sanpaolo's investments. One institution, four sites.
x: Records
It posts nothing itself; owner Intesa Sanpaolo posts annual reports and accounts for 2007 to 2025 and names its board, with no donor list.

f: 2025 income EUR 11.7M. Fondazione CR Firenze gave 1.1M, the Partners Committee 928k, the Recordati foundation 600k, Intesa Sanpaolo 464k. City, Region and Metropolitan City gave 500k each.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Enegan, a Florence retailer of gas and power, is a Partner and has supplied the Fondazione's renewable electricity since 2021. Visitors in 2025: 384,176.
x: Records
Reports run from 2007 to 2025, accounts with a KPMG audit are posted, the 2025 report names funders with amounts, and the board is listed.

n: Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana
f: Private. Pinault bought Palazzo Grassi in 2005 (EUR 29M). The City of Venice owns Punta della Dogana; he holds it on a 33-year agreement and paid its EUR 20M restoration.
w: Bottega Veneta, a Kering house, solely backs the 2026 Lorna Simpson show. Kering paid EUR 1.25bn in 2019 to settle an Italian tax case.

f: 2022 revenue EUR 11.4M: Ministry of Culture 2.9M, other public grants 5.3M, tickets 2.1M. Eni was an institutional partner and Main Partner of the 23rd Exhibition, with Lavazza.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. 661,234 visitors in 2022. Eni was also Main Sponsor of Progetto Genesi at Triennale in 2023, run by Associazione Genesi.
x: Records
Its site blocked fetches; search listings show reports and accounts for 2006 to 2025, partners named without a date, and a named board.

n: Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea
f: Ministry of Culture state museum. The ministry paid EUR 1.5M for its 2024-25 Futurism show. Main sponsors were Autostrade per l'Italia and Enel; Ferrovie dello Stato and Unipol also sponsored.
w: Enel made 82% of its 2025 power emission-free but runs gas plants. Autostrade per l'Italia held the Genoa bridge concession when it fell in 2018.

f: 2024 income EUR 33.2M: subsidies 19.7M, tickets 5.5M, sponsors 688k. Listed sponsors: JTI, Fundación Mutua Madrileña, Mastercard, Uber, Comunidad de Madrid. JTI gave EUR 59,328 for the 2024 Quintanilla show.
w: Flags: Tobacco. JTI has sponsored Thyssen shows since 2014 and is on the current sponsors page. Fundación Iberdrola, ACS and Bankinter also sponsor.
x: Records
Activity reports run 2017 to 2024, audited accounts 2013 to 2025 are posted, the 2024 accounts name sponsors with amounts, and the Patronato is listed.

f: Fundación la Caixa, paid by dividends from its holding Criteria; 2025 budget EUR 655M, about 130M for culture and science. CaixaForum Madrid had 947,642 visitors in 2024.
w: Gas utility Naturgy paid Criteria EUR 434M of its EUR 1,883M dividends in 2025. No source names Naturgy as a CaixaForum sponsor.

f: Run by Fundación Botín. Patrons: Fundación Mutua Madrileña, Fundación Prosegur, Roche España and two public tourism bodies. Strategic sponsors: Fundación EDP, Plenitude (Eni) and CESINE.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Plenitude, controlled by Eni, sells gas and power in Spain from Santander. Fundación EDP is also a strategic sponsor. No protest found.
x: Records
Fundación Botín posts annual reports from 2007 to 2025 and its trustees; the Centro Botín sponsor page names patrons and sponsors, undated.

f: Run by the Generalitat Valenciana's culture department; no operating budget found. 202,258 visitors in 2025. It bought 16 works by 14 women artists for about EUR 1M.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment. Director Enguita resigned in February 2024 after the Vox-led culture department, which funds IVAM, reported her land donation to prosecutors. They archived it in March.
x: Records
No annual report; accounts for 2012 to 2025 with audit reports are posted, the Consejo Rector is listed, and sponsors appear only as two logos.

f: Private foundation endowed by oilman Calouste Gulbenkian's fortune; assets EUR 4.0bn at end 2025. It owned oil firm Partex until selling it to PTTEP in November 2019.
w: Flags: Fossil fuels. Partex was about 18% of its investments. Ten protesters entered a Foundation conference in March 2016 and cited its ownership of Partex.
x: Records
Annual reports with certified accounts run from 2012 to 2025 and the board is listed; it publishes no donor list.

n: MAC/CCB Museu de Arte Contemporânea do Centro Cultural de Belém
f: Run by Fundação CCB, whose bodies the Culture and Finance ministers appoint. The State Budget gives about EUR 10.5M; the 2025 subsidy was unchanged. MAC/CCB had 588,643 visitors in 2024.
w: Flags: State censorship or punishment, Protest or boycott. The Culture Minister removed CCB president Francisca Carneiro Fernandes in November 2024. A petition drew 2,000+ signatures; in 2026 the State admitted no grounds.
x: Records
Reports run 2021 to 2025, with audited accounts in the 2024 one; a 2023 to 2025 table of support names funders; the board is listed.

f: Run by the Alexander S. Onassis Foundation, funded entirely by profits of its Business Foundation, which invests in shipping and real estate. Corporate sponsors exist; no budget is published.
w: Onassis built his fortune on tankers chartered to oil majors: no flag. Teachers stopped work in February 2025 against the Foundation's Onassis Public Schools.

f: Private foundation set up in Geneva in 1983 by collector Dakis Joannou, a construction and hotel businessman. No sponsor list, donor list or budget is published.
w: Runs the Athens space and the Slaughterhouse Project Space on Hydra, granted by the island's municipality in 2008. NEON belongs to Daskalopoulos, not Joannou.
x: Records
DESTE's About page names no donors or sponsors, and the site publishes no annual reports, accounts or board.

f: Nicosia Municipality and the Pierides Foundation run it under a cooperation agreement. Shows credit the Deputy Ministry of Culture, A.G. Leventis Foundation and European University Cyprus. No budget is published.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. A 2026 show with Emin Cizenel, who designed the north's flag, drew a small protest and a deputy mayor's call to cancel. No cancellation reported.
x: Records
One annual report covers 2024 and 2025; no accounts, funder list or board appear, though exhibition pages credit funders.

n: MICAS Malta International Contemporary Art Space
f: A EUR 30M project funded by the Maltese state and the European Regional Development Fund; the gallery works were co-financed 80% EU, 20% national. No sponsors are named.
w: A EUR 0.5M Rondinone sculpture was bought with no public call via board member Francis Sultana, who sells Rondinone. The minister denies a conflict.

f: Owned by Superstruct Entertainment, which KKR acquired in 2024. Its site shows the Generalitat, Estrella Damm and drinks brands. Sónar says it sends KKR no money. No budget found.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. In June 2025 at least 34 acts, including Arca and Rone, withdrew over KKR's Israel investments and its stake in Sónar's owner.
x: Records
It posts no reports, accounts or board; the site footer shows partner logos, undated, including Estrella Damm, Fritz-kola, the Generalitat and Barcelona City Council.

f: Greek state museum. The ministry assured EUR 42M of the EUR 59M expansion (2021). The Stavros Niarchos Foundation gave EUR 13M in 2017.
w: Flags: Protest or boycott. March 2025: MP Nikos Papadopoulos damaged four works he called blasphemous. September: 400 believers sought a court ban on the show; refused.
x: Records
It posts no annual reports, accounts or sponsor list; its structure page names the board of directors, and its footer links to the Diavgeia register.

f: Produced by Kampala Arts Trust and Afriart Gallery. KAB20 (2020) was co-funded by the EU and Pro Helvetia. TotalEnergies Foundation backed the 2018 mentoring programme; no later TotalEnergies money found.
w: Founded in 2014 by Daudi Karungi. No edition since the virtual KAB20 in 2020; the site is now an archive.

f: Produced by Desta for Africa, directed by Aida Muluneh. The last sponsor list is from 2018: Swiss Embassy, Canon, National Geographic Society, Marriott and others. None published since.
w: Founded 2010. The fifth edition opened 6 December 2018. A sixth was announced for December 2020; no edition since is documented.
x: Records
addisfotofest.com lists no sponsors, reports, accounts or board; it posts festival catalogues for 2010 to 2018 and names Desta for Africa as producer.

f: Owned and run by the Rwanda Cultural Heritage Academy, the government body that runs Rwanda's national museums. It charges entry fees; no sponsors are listed.
w: Opened in 2009 in the former presidential palace at Kanombe and renamed the Rwanda Art Museum in 2018.

f: Artist-run centre founded in 2012 by painter brothers Innocent Nkurunziza and Emmanuel Nkuranga. It runs a gallery, classes, tours, memberships and a café; no funders or sponsors are named.
w: Ten resident-artist slots at KG 563 St, Kacyiru. A funder list is not published.
x: Records
Inema's site names its two founders but no funders, reports, accounts or board; a Support Inema page exists but was not readable.

f: Funded privately by founder Hassanein Hiridjee, Axian's chief executive, who chairs it. Partners: Air France, Cité internationale des arts, Ravinala Airports, Fondation Axian, Interreg Océan Indien.
w: Name to know: founder's Axian group. Axian Energy (USD 510M, 18.5% of USD 2.75bn in 2024, with solar and hydro) runs 135 Jovena and Eydon fuel stations; telecom leads.

f: Won Culture Resource's Abbara Program grant (round 7, 2022). The Australian Government and Creative Australia support its Qubit fellowship (2026). The Spanish Embassy is a named partner.
w: Opened Muse Gallery in Khartoum in 2022; since the April 2023 war it works between Sudan and Egypt and runs the Sudan Art Archive.

n: Institute of Contemporary Art Indian Ocean (ICAIO)
f: Founded in 2015 by Salim Currimjee, a painter, architect and collector. No funder or sponsor list is published.
w: Exhibitions change each quarter, showing Mauritian, Indian and South African artists, at 51 Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Street, Port Louis.
x: Records
icaio.org now redirects to an unrelated gambling site, so ICAIO's own pages could not be read.

f: Operates under the Women's Gallery Arts and Research Trust. Its March 2023 show had support from the Swiss and Australian embassies and UN Women. No funder list is published.
w: Gallery Delta was founded in 1975 by Derek Huggins and Helen Lieros, who died in 2021; Nhaka presents itself as continuing that legacy.
x: Records
No Nhaka Gallery website was found; the only named backers are for one 2023 show, and no reports, accounts or board appear.

f: Founder Victor Mutelekesha's household paid for the building. Pro Helvetia paid for shelving; OCA, a Norwegian arts body, part-financed the 2023 opening show; the late artist Jan Groth donated.
w: Opened 6 January 2023 in New Chamba Valley with a gallery, library and artist residency; first show Prospice, Kwacha!

f: Artists' association with over 100 members. State funding ended in the civil war; a late-1990s profile names Hivos as donor. No current funder list is published.
w: Official foundation 1948; reopened in 1993 by young artists. Maputo's council and the CTA led a 2021 mural project with 40 of its members.
x: Records
The association's only page found is a late-1990s profile naming Hivos; it publishes no reports, accounts, funder list or board.

f: Funded by Wissam and Hiba Nesr. Wissam is chief executive of Webcor Group, a Swiss-based food importer and distributor with most African revenue in Angola. No outside funders named.
w: Opened in 2021 with a residency for Angolan and Lusophone African artists; the artistic committee is chaired by Paula Nascimento.

f: Binational centre under Namibian law, funded by the French government. Namibia gave the land and France paid for the building; foundation stone laid in 1998.
w: Has a large multipurpose gallery and hosts exhibitions at 118 Robert Mugabe Avenue, Windhoek.

n: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery
f: Statutory museum set up by Act of Parliament in 1967 and run by the Department of National Museum and Monuments. Government funded its P33 million refurbishment, begun in 2020.
w: Includes the National Art Gallery and the Octagon Gallery. Opened to the public in 1968.

n: Musée des Cultures Contemporaines Adama Toungara (MuCAT)
f: Built on the initiative of Adama Toungara, then mayor of Abobo; the director says it was built from own funds. No funder, cost or sponsor list is published.
w: Stands opposite Abobo town hall on 3,500 m², designed by architect Issa Diabaté. Opened with the pan-African show Prête-moi ton rêve.
x: Records
MuCAT's site lists a team but no board, partners, reports or accounts; it says the museum is private, foundation-owned and gets no state subsidy.

n: Festival International des Arts du Bénin (FInAB)
f: Run by Groupe Empire's events arm with Benin government support through its arts fund (FDAC). MTN partnered the 2026 edition, Canal+ Impact 2025. Other partners unnamed; no budget published.
w: Festival in Cotonou, Porto-Novo and Ouidah. The fourth edition closed in early March 2026, with days for Nigeria, Togo, Lebanon and Morocco.
x: Records
No FInAB website was found; press names organiser Groupe Empire, the culture ministry and different sponsors each year, with no reports, accounts or board.

f: Founded by Andrew Munuwa with Valentin Rudloff. The National Arts Council (BASATA) says it is keen to support it; no funder or sponsor list is published.
w: Launched in 2023. The 2025 edition showed 15 artists from Congo, Sudan, Kenya and Tanzania in Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar.
x: Records
The festival's site darfotofestival.com did not resolve, so nothing was checked; a fundraising page shows individual donors only.

f: Texaf, listed on Euronext Brussels, is founder and head sponsor of the centre. Its income is 85% Kinshasa real estate, 12% a sandstone quarry and 3% digital.
w: Texaf is 62.9% held by Société Financière Africaine and 10% by the Cha family. Bilembo covers over 1,000 m² of exhibition and workshop space.

f: Burkina Faso's culture ministry organises it and pays professional artists' fees, flights and stay, per its 2024 call for applications. No other funder is named.
w: Founded 1989 by Siriki Ky, 35 km from Ouagadougou. The 15th edition runs 2 to 23 November 2026 under President Traoré's patronage.

f: Eastern Cape government, Sarah Baartman District Municipality, National Lottery Commission, Standard Bank. National government gave R5.5 million for 2022 to 2024, nothing in 2025, a smaller grant in 2026.
w: Minister McKenzie says it lost an open call. A January 2026 petition of 302 artists cites the cut among his refusals to renew funding.

n: Javett Art Centre at the University of Pretoria (Javett-UP)
f: University of Pretoria gave the land and funding. The Javett Foundation funded construction and pledged ten years of annual gifts for running costs and an endowment.
w: Opened September 2019. An independent trust runs it. Michael Javett founded the Unisec Group, later sold to Standard Bank, and Tolux, now Brait.

f: Private firm of Nadine Abdel Ghaffar. Egypt's foreign and tourism ministries and UNESCO sponsor Forever Is Now. Partners: LMD, Suez Canal Bank, BMW (2026); TotalEnergies, Afreximbank (2024).
w: Flags: Fossil fuels, Protest or boycott. In October 2026 a petition of 500 to 700 signatories made it drop sculptor Bernar Venet over Israeli ties; artists and galleries withdrew.
x: Records
It posts no reports or accounts; the site shows four logos of ministries and UNESCO, undated, and lists a three-person team but no board.

f: Primarily funded by the Yinka Shonibare Foundation at its 2019 launch. Donors include Terra Foundation, Deutsche Bank, Afreximbank, Still Earth Holdings, British Council and Pro Helvetia.
w: Founded 2019 by Yinka Shonibare, who started the London residency Guest Projects. Patron Still Earth Holdings owns drilling contractor Tirex, an oil-services supplier.

f: Art network and incubator tied to the KNUST painting and sculpture department in Kumasi. No funders, sponsors or budget appear in any source opened.
w: Ranked 69 in ArtReview's 2025 Power 100 and invited to the 2026 Venice Biennale main exhibition.
x: Records
No blaxTARLINES website was found; Wikipedia lists none and no source names a funder, report, accounts or board.

f: Trust founded in 1995. Swedish NGO donor Forum Syd commissioned a 2016 audit. Robert Devereux's African Arts Trust aimed to become a patron in 2012. No current funder list.
w: Closed its offices in September 2016 for a donor audit after multi-million shillings went missing; artists kept the centre running.
x: Records
kuonatrust.org returned HTTP 500, so nothing could be checked; a search found no annual report, funders or trustees.

f: Founded with private money by Boubacar Koné and actress CCH Pounder; Koné gave it to the Senegalese state in December 2014. No budget or sponsor list is published.
w: Ngor museum of contemporary African art with artist studios and a residency. A conservator from the Ministry of Culture took office in March 2015.
x: Records
The ministry page on Boribana gives its history and 2014 state handover but no budget, reports, accounts, funders or board.

n: Contemporary Art Museum of the Kasbah
f: Run by the National Foundation of Museums. Restoration and design cost 13 million dirhams; the Wilaya of Tangier supervised it, with the Ministry of Culture, APDN and the Foundation contributing.
w: Opened in December 2021 in the former Kasbah prison to mark the Foundation's tenth anniversary. Opening show: The School of the North.
